# Tutezy vs Khanmigo
Khanmigo is Khan Academy’s AI tutor for its own curriculum, aimed at individual learners, parents and (mostly US) classroom teachers. Tutezy teaches an institute’s own material, in its own teacher’s voice, and reports back to the institute. They solve different problems.

The short version

- ✦ Khanmigo: a well-designed Socratic tutor on Khan Academy’s curriculum, for individuals and schools using that curriculum.
- ✦ Tutezy: a live whiteboard teacher compiled from your content, for institutes that need it taught their way and reported back.
- ✦ If your students learn Khan Academy’s syllabus, Khanmigo is excellent and cheap. If they learn yours, it cannot help.
- ✦ Tutezy also speaks Hindi, clones your teacher’s voice and bills the institute per minute rather than the learner per month.

## What Khanmigo is
Khanmigo is the AI tutor and teaching assistant built by Khan Academy, a non-profit. It guides learners through Khan Academy’s own courses with Socratic questioning rather than answers, helps with practice problems on the platform, and gives teachers lesson-planning and grading assistance. It is priced for individual learners and families at a small monthly fee, and offered to teachers in some countries at no cost. It is tied to Khan Academy’s curriculum and interface; it does not ingest a third-party institute’s material.

## Side by side
  | Tutezy | Khanmigo |

Curriculum | Yours: whatever you upload and compile | Khan Academy’s courses |
Who it is sold to | Institutes, schools, creators, trainers; billed per learner-minute | Individual learners and families; teachers in some regions |
Medium | Live whiteboard drawn as the teacher speaks, plus voice | Chat beside Khan Academy content and exercises |
Teacher identity | Your teacher’s name, cloned voice, optional avatar | A Khan Academy character |
Languages | English and Hindi, switchable mid-lesson | Primarily English, with some localisation |
Checks and remediation | Rubric-graded checks per concept, hints, revisits, next-lesson recap | Socratic prompts on Khan exercises |
Reports | Per student and per batch, to your institute, CSV | Learner progress within Khan Academy; teacher tools for Khan classrooms |
Fit for Indian exam prep, corporate training, certification | Yes, from your own material | No — outside its curriculum |
Price | ₹3 / $0.03 per learner-minute; no seats | Small monthly fee per learner (see khanmigo.ai) |

## Choose Khanmigo when

- The learner is studying Khan Academy’s courses and wants a tutor on them.
- A parent wants an affordable, safe tutor for general school maths and science at home.
- A school uses Khan Academy as its curriculum and wants its teacher tools.

## Choose Tutezy when

- The material is yours: coaching modules, school worksheets, a creator’s course, a corporate deck, a university’s notes.
- The teaching must be in the institute’s teacher’s voice and method, and reviewed before students see it.
- You need mastery reports per student and per batch back at the institute.
- Students need Hindi, or a mid-lesson switch between Hindi and English.
- You want to be billed for minutes taught, not per learner per month.

## The real difference: whose content, whose teacher, whose report
A consumer AI tutor comes with a curriculum, a persona and a learner account. That is exactly right for a family. An institute needs the opposite on all three counts: its own syllabus (down to the notation and shortcuts its faculty use), its own teacher’s identity on the teaching, and a report that lands with the academic head. Tutezy is built around those three: content is compiled from the institute’s material and reviewed, the teacher is the institute’s (name, cloned voice, avatar, strictness), and every session writes mastery per concept that rolls up per batch. See what Tutezy is .
Descriptions of third-party products reflect public information as of September 2026 and may change; check the product’s own site for current features and pricing.

## Frequently asked questions
Can Tutezy teach Khan Academy content?+
Only if you have the rights to upload it. Tutezy compiles from material the institute provides; it does not ship a curriculum of its own.

Is Tutezy Socratic like Khanmigo?+
Partly. Tutezy teaches first — board and narration — then asks; wrong answers get a hint before the answer, and predict-then-reveal prompts ask for the next step before showing it. It is a teacher with a plan rather than a pure questioning tutor.

Which is cheaper?+
For one child at home, Khanmigo’s monthly fee is hard to beat. For an institute, Tutezy’s ₹3 per learner-minute means 20 minutes a day for a month is about ₹1,300 per student, with no per-learner licence and your own content.

Does Tutezy work for younger children?+
From roughly Class 4 upwards — children who can read a board and answer a question. Strictness and pace are adjustable.

# Tutezy vs recorded video courses | Tutezy

Comparison

# Tutezy vs recorded video courses
Recorded video is cheap to deliver and impossible to interrupt. It cannot ask whether the student understood, cannot notice confusion, and cannot explain the same thing a second way. Tutezy takes the same recordings and turns them into a lesson that can.

The short version

- ✦ Recorded courses: zero marginal cost, high production polish, single pace, no interaction, completion rates typically under 20%.
- ✦ Tutezy: the same content taught live one to one, with checks and remediation, at ₹3 a learner-minute.
- ✦ Not either/or: Tutezy compiles from your recordings. The video stays; a “learn with the teacher” button appears beside it.

## What recorded courses is
A recorded course is a sequence of videos, often with PDFs and quizzes, delivered through an LMS or a course platform. It is the dominant format for online learning because it scales for free once made. Its weakness is well documented: without a person in the loop most learners stop partway, and nobody knows what the ones who finished actually understood.

## Side by side
  | Tutezy | recorded courses |

Interaction | Teacher asks after every concept; student answers by voice or text; hints and revisits | None; play, pause, rewind |
Pace | Slower, slow, medium, fast; chosen by the student, remembered | Playback speed only |
Confusion | Detected by the check; remediated; revisited later | Invisible |
Doubts | Answered against the material, then back to the lesson | Forum or WhatsApp, hours later, if at all |
Language | English and Hindi compiled for every concept, switchable | Whichever language was recorded |
Teacher presence | Cloned voice; optional avatar; name and strictness | The recording |
What the institute learns | Mastery per concept per student; weak spots per batch | Watch time and completion |
Marginal cost | ₹3 / $0.03 per learner-minute | Near zero |
Production effort | Compile from existing recordings and PDFs; review boards | Script, shoot, edit, re-shoot when the syllabus changes |
Updating content | Edit the source and recompile the slide | Re-record |

## Choose recorded courses when

- The content is inspirational or narrative rather than something with checkable understanding.
- Learners are highly self-motivated and the institute does not need to know what they understood.
- Marginal cost must be zero and interaction is not needed.

## Choose Tutezy when

- Completion and understanding matter — exam prep, certification, compliance, a course sold on outcomes.
- The institute needs to know who is stuck on what.
- Students need to ask, to be asked, and to go at their own pace.
- A Hindi option is needed without re-recording.
- The syllabus changes and re-shooting is not practical.

## Keep the video. Add the teacher.
The usual objection is sunk cost: “we spent a year recording”. Tutezy does not throw that away. Recordings are transcribed and compiled into board lessons; the original video stays in the course; the student gets a button on the same chapter. Institutes typically start with the chapters where completion drops and expand from there. Setup is described on the how it works page; the per-minute economics on the pricing page .
Descriptions of third-party products reflect public information as of September 2026 and may change; check the product’s own site for current features and pricing.

## Frequently asked questions
Do we have to re-record anything?+
No. Existing videos are transcribed and compiled; PDFs and decks are read directly. You review the boards and recompile any you want tighter.

Does Tutezy replace the video?+
No. It sits beside it. Students can still watch; the lesson button opens the one-to-one teacher on the same chapter.

Is it pre-rendered like a video?+
No. The board is drawn live from the compiled plan and the conversation is live, which is what lets it react to a wrong answer.

What does it cost compared with video?+
Video is free per view; Tutezy is ₹3 per learner-minute. A 30-minute chapter costs ₹90 per student. Most institutes charge for or fund it from the completion and retention gain.

# Tutezy vs one-to-one human tutoring | Tutezy
URL: https://tutezy.ai/compare/tutezy-vs-human-tutoring/

- Home
- › Compare
- › Tutezy vs human tutoring
Comparison

# Tutezy vs one-to-one human tutoring
A good human tutor is the best form of teaching there is, and Tutezy is modelled on what they do. The human is also the scarcest resource in every institute. Tutezy is built to take the repetitive one-to-one work between live sessions, and to tell the human exactly where they are needed.

The short version

- ✦ Human tutor: judgment, motivation, relationship, improvisation. ₹300–₹1,500+ an hour, one student at a time, limited hours.
- ✦ Tutezy: the explain–ask–check–revisit loop, in the teacher’s voice, for every student at once, ₹180 an hour each, any hour.
- ✦ The design goal is not to replace the tutor but to multiply them and to route their hours to the students who need them.

## What human tutoring is
One-to-one human tutoring is a teacher and a student, live, working through material with immediate feedback. It is the reference standard: decades of research put one-to-one tutoring well ahead of classroom instruction. Its constraints are cost, availability and consistency — the best tutors are booked, the affordable ones vary, and no institute can give every student an hour a day.

## Side by side
  | Tutezy | human tutoring |

Judgment and improvisation | Within a compiled plan; hints, revisits, doubt answers | Unlimited; reads the room, changes approach |
Motivation and relationship | Familiar teacher voice and name; patient, never tired; no relationship | The main reason many students keep going |
Consistency | Every student gets the same reviewed board | Varies by tutor and by day |
Availability | Any hour, every student at once, resumes where they stopped | Booked slots; one student per slot |
Language | English and Hindi, switchable mid-lesson | Depends on the tutor |
Record of learning | Mastery per concept, transcript, notes, batch roll-up, CSV | The tutor’s memory and a verbal update |
Cost | ₹3 / $0.03 per learner-minute (₹180 an hour) | ₹300–₹1,500+ an hour in India; more abroad |
Scale | A batch of 500 at once | One |
Handles the unexpected | Answers doubts about the material; returns to the plan | Anything |

## Choose human tutoring when

- The student needs mentoring, motivation or a relationship more than explanation.
- The material is open-ended: research, projects, essays, portfolio work.
- A student’s difficulty is not about the content — the human should have that conversation.
- The budget allows an hour a day per student and the tutors are available.

## Choose Tutezy when

- Every student in a batch needs the explain–ask–check–revisit loop and there is one teacher.
- The repetitive part of tutoring — homework help, practice, revision, solution sessions — is eating the human’s hours.
- The institute wants to know, before the live session, who is stuck on what.
- Students need help at 11 pm, on a phone, in Hindi or English.
- The cost per student-hour must be a fraction of a human tutor’s.

## How institutes use both
The pattern that works: the human teaches the live class and keeps office hours; Tutezy takes the daily practice, the post-test solution sessions and the late-night doubts, in the teacher’s own voice; each morning the teacher sees the batch’s weak concepts and the individual students flagged, and spends the human hour on them. Faculty stop repeating the same explanation two hundred times and start doing the part only a human can. See the coaching institute and independent tutor pages for worked examples.
Descriptions of third-party products reflect public information as of September 2026 and may change; check the product’s own site for current features and pricing.

## Frequently asked questions
Is Tutezy meant to replace teachers?+
No. It multiplies them. Your teachers’ content, name, voice and face teach every student one to one, and the teacher sees who needs them in person.

Can it motivate a discouraged student the way a person can?+
Not the way a person can. It is patient, familiar-sounding and never sighs, which helps; but a student who needs a human conversation should get one, and Tutezy’s flags help the teacher find that student.

How does the cost compare?+
₹3 per learner-minute is ₹180 an hour, against ₹300–₹1,500 an hour for a human tutor in India. The bigger difference is that Tutezy teaches the whole batch at once.

Do teachers resist it?+
Less than expected once they see it uses their own material and voice, reports to them, and takes the repetitive work off their evenings. Likeness use is consent-gated and can be disabled at any time.

Buyer's guide

# AI math tutors: teaching beyond the final answer
An AI math tutor should help a learner choose and explain the next step, then solve a fresh problem independently. For schools and tutoring businesses, the useful buying question is whether the tool reveals mathematical thinking and responds to mistakes—not simply whether it can produce a correct solution.
By the Tutezy team · October 10, 2026 · 5 min read

Key takeaways

- ✦ Evaluate the learner’s work as well as the tutor’s answer.
- ✦ Use a worked example, a partially completed problem and an independent problem.
- ✦ Check equivalent answers, notation and the reason behind each operation.
- ✦ Measure success with fresh questions completed without hints.
In this article

- What to look for
- A worked algebra lesson
- Responding to mistakes
- A practical evaluation checklist
- Run a small pilot

## What should an AI math tutor actually teach?
A useful math lesson connects a procedure to its meaning. A student who can repeat “move the three to the other side” may still be unsure why an equation stays balanced. Ask the tutor to explain the operation on both sides, show it clearly and invite the learner to apply it. The explanation should match the notation and methods used in class.
The Institute of Education Sciences practice guide recommends alternating worked solutions with problems learners solve themselves. That principle offers a sensible starting point for lesson design; it does not establish that any particular AI product improves achievement.
Before comparing tools, choose a narrow use case: early algebra practice, fractions revision or support between tutoring sessions. Bring your own examples, including a valid alternative method and a plausible wrong answer. A polished demonstration with an easy question reveals little about how the tutor will handle your students’ work.

## A step-by-step algebra lesson you can adapt
Suppose the objective is to solve a two-step linear equation and justify each operation. Start by checking that the learner can solve a one-step equation such as x + 4 = 9. If that is insecure, address it before adding multiplication.
Stage | Example | What the learner contributes |

Worked example | 2x + 3 = 11 → 2x = 8 → x = 4 | Explain why subtracting 3 from both sides preserves equality. |
Partial example | 3x + 2 = 14 → 3x = 12 → … | Complete the division and check the result in the original equation. |
Independent practice | 5x − 4 = 16 | Choose the operations, obtain x = 4 and verify 5 × 4 − 4 = 16. |
Application | A hire fee is $6 plus $3 per hour. The total is $21. | Write 3h + 6 = 21, solve h = 5 and explain what h means. |

Reveal the solution after the learner has attempted the relevant step. Then ask a new question: repeating an answer that is still on the board is weak evidence of learning. Keep a separate record of whether the learner answered independently, after a hint or after seeing the complete method.

## Respond to the particular mistake
If a learner changes 2x + 3 = 11 into 2x = 14, the issue may be the inverse operation. Ask, “Which operation would undo adding three?” If they reach 2x = 8 and answer x = 6, ask what 2x means before presenting another equation. These errors need different explanations.
Try this error check
Show the deliberately incorrect line “3(x + 2) = 3x + 2.” Ask the student to expand it, identify the missing multiplication and test both expressions at x = 1. Finish with the corrected expression, 3x + 6.

Do not force every wrong response into a conceptual diagnosis. A learner may mistype, misread a minus sign or have trouble entering a fraction. Ask for clarification when notation is ambiguous. A tool that interprets spoken mathematics should confirm the expression before evaluating it.

## Use this evaluation checklist

- Mathematical accuracy: check every displayed step, including negative signs and units.
- Equivalent forms: test whether 0.5 and 1/2 are accepted where both meet the question’s requirements.
- Useful feedback: submit a wrong intermediate step and inspect the response.
- Alternative methods: try a correct approach that differs from the prepared solution.
- Teacher visibility: look for the concept causing trouble and the amount of support used.
- Limits: check what happens when the question is ambiguous or outside the prepared lesson.
For a broader procurement review, use our AI tutoring software checklist . Verify specialist capabilities such as handwriting recognition or symbolic equivalence directly with the provider; a conversational interface alone does not establish either.

## Run a small pilot around one learning objective
Choose one class topic and prepare a short independent task before tutoring. After a week of targeted practice, use different questions testing the same skills. Add a delayed check the following week and review a sample of lesson interactions for incorrect feedback. Track teacher review time alongside learner performance.
A small pilot can reveal usability problems and suggest whether the approach is useful locally. Differences in prior knowledge, practice time and teacher support make it a poor basis for a broad causal claim. Decide what would justify continuing before seeing the results.
Where Tutezy fits

## What we built for this
Tutezy builds live whiteboard lessons from an educator’s content, with questions, hints and concept-level feedback. For a math pilot, bring a reviewed chapter and examples of the mistakes you want to address. See Tutezy for schools or support for independent tutors .

## Sources

- IES, Organizing Instruction and Study to Improve Student Learning (2007). ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/PracticeGuide/1

## Frequently asked questions
What is an AI math tutor?+
An AI math tutor provides explanations, practice and feedback in mathematics. Capabilities vary: some tools mainly solve submitted problems, while others guide a planned lesson. Check whether students must attempt steps and whether the tutor tests independent understanding.

Can an AI math tutor replace a teacher?+
Use it for selected practice and follow-up within a teacher-led course. Teachers still need to choose the curriculum, check explanations, interpret persistent difficulties and decide when a student needs a different approach.

How do I test whether a math tutor helps?+
Compare an initial independent task with new questions of similar difficulty after practice, then check again later. Record the hints used during tutoring so a supported answer is not mistaken for independent success.

# AI tutoring for STEM: from explanation to application | Tutezy

# AI tutoring for STEM: from explanation to application
AI tutoring for STEM works best as a planned sequence of explanation, prediction, calculation and application. Start with a specific learning objective, prepare the diagrams and examples carefully, and test whether students can use the idea in a new situation after the tutor’s support is removed.
By the Tutezy team · October 10, 2026 · 5 min read

Key takeaways

- ✦ Choose an observable outcome, such as explaining a graph or predicting a change.
- ✦ Connect equations, diagrams and words within the same example.
- ✦ Use predictions and debugging tasks to make reasoning visible.
- ✦ Keep practical work and independent assessment in the course.
In this article

- The tutor’s role in STEM
- Physics: interpret before calculating
- Biology and coding examples
- Prepare your content
- Evaluate a STEM pilot

## Where AI tutoring can fit in STEM education
A learner can watch an explanation of acceleration and still confuse speed with acceleration. STEM teaching needs moments where students commit to a prediction, connect representations or explain a result. An individual tutoring session offers room for those exchanges between classes, provided the lesson is designed around them.
Freeman and colleagues’ 2014 meta-analysis compared active learning with traditional lecturing across 225 undergraduate STEM studies. It found better examination performance and lower failure rates with active learning. Those studies examined varied teaching approaches, not modern generative AI tutors; the findings support student participation, not a product-specific promise.
Our suggested starting point is a single difficult concept with a clear endpoint. Replace “understand motion” with “interpret the slope of a straight distance-time graph for constant speed.” A narrow target makes content review and assessment more manageable.

## Physics: interpret the situation before calculating
Consider a cyclist travelling at a constant speed of 4 metres per second. A tutoring sequence can move through the same situation in several forms. State that the model assumes constant speed so students know where the equation applies.
Prompt | Expected reasoning | What to check |

How far will the cyclist travel in 3 seconds? | 4 metres each second gives 12 metres. | Distance, time and speed are distinguished. |
What does the distance-time graph look like? | A straight line with constant slope, starting at zero for this example. | The learner connects constant speed with constant slope. |
How would the graph change at 8 metres per second? | The line becomes twice as steep on the same axes. | The learner interprets slope rather than height alone. |
What if the cyclist stops? | Distance stays constant while time continues. | A horizontal segment is distinguished from returning to the start. |

Have the learner describe or sketch the graph before revealing it. Then present a different graph and ask for an interpretation. If the learner calculates correctly but cannot explain a flat segment, address graph meaning rather than assigning more multiplication.
For equations with several variables, keep symbols, units and assumptions visible. Ask for the unit of the answer before accepting it. For more detail on checking intermediate work, see our guide to AI math tutors .

## Apply the same approach to biology and coding

### Biology: separate prediction from explanation
Provide a teacher-reviewed diagram of photosynthesis and ask the learner to label the inputs and outputs. Next, present a simple scenario: the light source is removed while other conditions stay the same. Ask what happens to photosynthesis and why. Follow with a separate question about respiration to check whether the learner treats the two processes as interchangeable.
For an investigation using supplied data, ask students to identify the variable changed, the measured outcome and a limitation of the conclusion. Keep the source of the data clear. An invented example can teach interpretation, but should be labelled as illustrative rather than presented as a real experiment.

### Coding: trace a short program before running it
Give students a loop over the list [2, 4, 6] that starts with total = 0 and adds each value. Ask for the value of total after each iteration, then ask what changes if the initial value becomes 10. The answers are 2, 6 and 12 in the first case, with a final total of 22 in the second.
Only then introduce a small bug and ask the learner to locate it. Use the course’s coding environment to execute the program where needed; do not assume a tutor can run or verify code unless that capability has been demonstrated.

## Prepare STEM material for a tutoring lesson

- State the objective and the prior knowledge it requires.
- Check diagram labels, graph axes, symbols and units in the source material.
- Provide a worked example and acceptable alternative explanations.
- List likely mistakes with a targeted hint for each.
- Add one fresh application question that students have not already seen.
Review the actual lesson
A correct slide does not guarantee a correct tutoring exchange. Preview the displayed diagrams and deliberately submit a mistaken answer. Check both the feedback and what happens next.

The IES practice guide recommends combining visual and verbal explanations and linking concrete examples to abstract representations. Apply that principle deliberately: decorative images and equations disconnected from the example add little instructional value.

## Evaluate one STEM unit before expanding
Begin with a unit that teachers already assess. Collect a short baseline task, offer focused tutoring and assess the objective with new questions. Include an explanation or unfamiliar application, since a repeated calculation may reveal memorization alone. Check again after a delay.
Review incorrect tutor feedback, unresolved misconceptions and staff preparation time. Keep hands-on work, discussion and teacher support in place. Expand only when the lesson is accurate and the workflow produces information teachers can use.

Tutezy turns existing teaching material into live whiteboard lessons with questions and follow-up support. A practical trial starts with one reviewed STEM chapter. Explore Tutezy for universities , schools or the lesson workflow .

## Sources

- Freeman et al., Active learning increases student performance in science, engineering, and mathematics (2014). pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4060654
- IES, Organizing Instruction and Study to Improve Student Learning (2007). ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/PracticeGuide/1

## Frequently asked questions
Which STEM topics are suitable for AI tutoring?+
Begin with a bounded topic that has reviewed explanations, clear diagrams and questions a teacher can check, such as interpreting motion graphs, explaining a biological process or tracing a short program. Evaluate the tutor on that topic before expanding.

Can an AI tutor replace a science lab?+
A tutor can help students prepare predictions and interpret supplied results. Handling equipment, making observations, following lab procedures and working with other students still require suitable practical learning experiences.

How should STEM educators measure success?+
Use fresh questions that require prediction, explanation or application without tutor help. Review accuracy, recurring misconceptions and teacher workload as well as completion and time spent.

# Diagnostic assessment for personalized learning | Tutezy

Learning science

# Diagnostic assessment for personalized learning
A diagnostic assessment identifies the knowledge a learner needs next and the misconceptions that may block progress. To turn it into personalized learning, connect each result to a specific teaching response, then check whether the learner can apply the idea independently. A score alone is not a learning plan.
By the Tutezy team · October 10, 2026 · 5 min read

Key takeaways

- ✦ Start with the prerequisites for the next unit, not a test of everything taught so far.
- ✦ Pair selected answers with a short explanation to distinguish errors from guesses.
- ✦ Attach a teaching action and a follow-up question to each identified gap.
- ✦ Use results as provisional evidence and revisit them after support.
In this article

- Diagnostic, formative and summative assessment
- A sample fraction diagnostic
- Turn results into a learning plan
- Where an AI tutor can help
- Review the assessment itself

## Diagnostic, formative and summative assessment: what changes?
The distinction is the decision the assessment supports. A diagnostic check asks what the learner brings to a topic and what may need attention first. Formative assessment guides changes during teaching. Summative assessment records achievement at the end of a unit or course. The same question can serve different purposes depending on when and how its answer is used.
For example, a fractions question before a ratio unit can reveal a prerequisite gap. During the unit it can guide the next explanation. At the end it may contribute to a grade. A diagnostic result should lead to support, rather than becoming a permanent label about a learner’s ability.
The Education Endowment Foundation’s mastery learning guidance includes diagnostic assessment, sequencing, feedback and additional support as connected parts of implementation. It also describes limited evidence and variation in outcomes. Buying an assessment tool alone does not implement that approach.

## Build a short diagnostic around a prerequisite
Imagine the next lesson involves comparing ratios, but students need secure fraction concepts first. Choose questions that separate specific ideas. The following examples are a starting point for teacher review, not a standardized assessment.
Question | Expected answer | Possible follow-up |

Which is larger, 1/3 or 1/5? Explain. | 1/3, because equal wholes divided into fewer equal pieces have larger pieces. | If 1/5 is chosen, compare two equally sized shaded bars. |
Complete 2/3 = ?/12. | 8/12; multiply numerator and denominator by 4. | Ask why changing both by the same factor preserves the value. |
Calculate 1/4 + 1/4. | 2/4 or 1/2. | If 2/8 is given, count quarter-sized pieces using a diagram. |
Place 3/4 on a line from 0 to 1. | Three of four equal intervals from zero. | Check whether the learner counts points or intervals. |

A wrong response suggests a follow-up; it does not prove its cause. A student who selects 1/5 may have read too quickly. Someone who answers correctly may have guessed. Ask for a brief explanation or a second example before assigning substantial remedial work.
Keep the language simple and accept appropriate equivalent forms. Decide in advance whether simplification is required. If a check is about fraction meaning, rejecting 2/4 solely because it is not written as 1/2 can obscure the skill you intended to assess.

## Turn evidence into a personalized learning plan
Write the next action at the concept level. “Work on fractions” is too broad. “Compare unit fractions using equal-sized wholes, then explain a new pair without the diagram” tells a tutor what to do and gives the teacher a way to check progress.
Example learning-plan entry
Evidence: the learner chose 1/5 as larger than 1/3 and explained that five is larger than three.
Next activity: compare equal-sized bars divided into three and five equal parts, then explain what the denominator represents.
Independent check: compare 1/4 and 1/6, explaining why the wholes must be the same size.
Review: revisit the idea in the next lesson; if confusion persists, change the representation and involve the teacher.

Students who demonstrate the prerequisite can move to an application task. Students with different gaps should receive different short activities. Avoid sending everyone below a total-score threshold through the same full chapter: identical totals can hide very different needs.
Keep groups flexible. A learner may need support with a representation while reasoning confidently in another context. Record what was observed and when it was checked, rather than treating the group assignment as a stable description of the student.

## Where an AI tutor can help with follow-up
An AI tutor can provide practice on an educator-selected concept, ask for an explanation and offer a prepared hint. The useful handover includes the objective, the learner’s response, the relevant misconception and the criterion for trying a new question. A chapter title and a percentage score give much less guidance.
Check whether your chosen platform actually supports the diagnostic-to-lesson workflow you need. If results must be reviewed and assignments made manually, include that work in the rollout plan. Do not assume automatic placement, assessment import or timetable changes are available because a tool uses AI.
Use checks during the lesson to update the initial diagnosis. If a learner succeeds only after several hints, preserve that distinction in the teaching notes. Independent success and supported success call for different next steps.

## Review the diagnostic as well as the learner
If many students miss an item, examine the wording, diagram and accepted answer before concluding that the whole class lacks the concept. Ask a colleague to solve the questions and explain what each one measures. Review whether reading demands or unfamiliar notation are interfering with the intended skill.
After follow-up teaching, use new questions on the same concepts. Track which gaps were resolved, which require another approach and how much staff time the process takes. The result should be a manageable teaching decision for each learner, not a longer dashboard that nobody acts on.
Where Tutezy fits

## What we built for this
Tutezy’s lessons check understanding and report concept-level weak spots. Educators can use those signals alongside their own assessments to plan support. See how lessons work and Tutezy for coaching institutes before designing your follow-up workflow.

## Sources

- Education Endowment Foundation, Mastery learning: implementation and evidence overview. educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk/education-evidence/teaching-learning-toolkit/mastery-learning

## Frequently asked questions
What is the purpose of diagnostic assessment?+
It helps a teacher identify relevant prior knowledge, misconceptions and missing prerequisites before deciding what to teach next. Its value comes from changing the support a learner receives.

How long should a diagnostic assessment be?+
Use enough questions to inform the next teaching decision without making the check exhausting. For a small prerequisite check, a few carefully chosen questions may be sufficient. Add follow-up questions when an answer is ambiguous.

Can AI create a personalized learning plan?+
AI can assist with drafting activities and responding to practice answers. An educator should check the underlying questions, interpretation of results and proposed sequence. A generated plan should be revised as new evidence of learning appears.

# Socratic AI tutoring: questions that help students think | Tutezy
URL: https://tutezy.ai/blog/socratic-ai-tutor-questioning/

- Home
- ›
- Blog
- ›

Learning science

# Socratic AI tutoring: questions that help students think
A Socratic AI tutor uses questions to help learners explain a claim, inspect an assumption and connect evidence to a conclusion. Good questioning responds to what the student says. It also makes room for direct explanation when a learner lacks the knowledge needed to answer.
By the Tutezy team · October 10, 2026 · 5 min read

Key takeaways

- ✦ Ask one clear question with a teaching purpose at a time.
- ✦ Move from a broad prompt to a specific hint when the learner stalls.
- ✦ Teach missing knowledge instead of repeating questions indefinitely.
- ✦ Finish with a fresh independent task that checks the underlying idea.
In this article

- What Socratic tutoring means
- A sample tutoring dialogue
- Build a hint ladder
- When to explain directly
- Evaluate the conversation

## What does Socratic tutoring look like in practice?
Instead of accepting an unsupported answer, a tutor asks how the learner reached it. Instead of immediately correcting a claim, the tutor may introduce a case that tests it. The aim is to make reasoning visible and help the learner improve it. A conversation full of question marks can still fail at both.
The IES practice guide on instruction and study recommends deep explanatory questions. That supports asking students to explain ideas; it does not imply that every lesson should use questioning alone or that a tutor should refuse to provide information.
For an AI tutoring lesson, define the concept and likely misconceptions before writing the prompts. A question should help distinguish between plausible ways of thinking. “Can you think harder?” offers little direction. “What happens to the number of equal pieces when the denominator increases?” has a specific instructional purpose.

## A sample dialogue: comparing unit fractions
Here is an illustrative exchange for a learner who already knows the numerator and denominator. It compares fractions of equal-sized wholes, a condition the tutor must state explicitly.
Speaker | Dialogue | Teaching purpose |

Tutor | Two equal-sized pizzas are cut into four and eight equal slices. Which pizza has larger slices? | Make the comparison concrete. |
Learner | The one cut into eight, because eight is bigger. | Expose the rule the learner is using. |
Tutor | Imagine cutting each of the four slices in half. How many slices are there now, and what happened to their size? | Test the claim with a visible transformation. |
Learner | Eight slices, but each is smaller. | Connect piece count and piece size. |
Tutor | So which is larger, 1/4 or 1/8, when the wholes are equal? | Return to the original mathematical statement. |
Learner | 1/4. Each piece is bigger when there are fewer equal pieces. | State the corrected reasoning. |

Now ask the learner to compare 1/3 and 1/6 without the pizza example. Follow with a boundary question: can you compare the physical size of slices from two differently sized pizzas using the fractions alone? This checks both the rule and the condition under which the example works.
The dialogue is a teaching design example, not a transcript from a Tutezy session or evidence of a measured learning gain. Real students may respond in unexpected ways, so the tutor needs a way to clarify ambiguous responses.

## Build a hint ladder for difficult moments
A hint ladder makes support progressively more specific. Prepare the rungs around the actual concept so the tutor can help without jumping immediately to the full solution.

- Restate the target: “We are comparing the size of one piece from each equal-sized whole.”
- Point to the relevant feature: “Look at how many equal pieces each whole has.”
- Offer a representation: show equal-length bars divided into four and eight parts.
- Model the reasoning: explain the comparison, then ask the learner to try a new pair.
Record which support was needed. A correct response after the modelled explanation is a useful step, but it is not the same evidence as an independent explanation. Review that distinction when deciding whether to move on or revisit the concept.

## When should the tutor stop asking and explain?
If the learner does not know what the denominator means, questions about its effect may become a guessing game. Teach the vocabulary with a labelled example first. Direct explanation is also appropriate when the learner requests clarification, when several attempts repeat the same confusion or when the question itself was unclear.
Set a stopping rule
For a pilot lesson, a teacher might allow an initial attempt and two increasingly specific hints before offering an explanation. This is a starting rule to evaluate, not a research-backed universal limit. Watch for frustration and adapt sooner when needed.

Avoid stacking several questions in one turn. “What do you think, why, what rule applies, and what would happen next?” burdens the learner with deciding which question to answer. Ask one question, listen to the response and make the next move from that evidence.

## Evaluate the conversation, not its length
Review a few exchanges against five questions: Was the prompt clear? Did the response reveal thinking? Was the hint relevant? Did the tutor explain when needed? Could the learner solve a new task afterward? A long conversation is not automatically a productive one.
Also test correct but unexpected answers. A rigid tutor may reject valid reasoning because it does not match a prepared phrase. Include equivalent wording in your review set, and inspect how the system handles uncertainty. Our guide to grounding AI tutors in course material covers related accuracy checks.
Where Tutezy fits

## What we built for this
Tutezy combines explanations, understanding checks, hints and bounded remediation within lessons prepared from your content. Use a demo to inspect the questioning around one of your own misconceptions. See how Tutezy teaches or how tutors can use it between sessions .

## Sources

- IES, Organizing Instruction and Study to Improve Student Learning (2007), recommendation on explanatory questions. ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/PracticeGuide/1

## Frequently asked questions
What is Socratic AI tutoring?+
It is tutoring that uses purposeful questions to draw out a learner’s reasoning, examine assumptions and help them connect ideas. In practice, it should combine questioning with explanations and examples when needed.

Should a Socratic tutor always withhold the answer?+
No. If a learner lacks a prerequisite or remains confused after a useful hint, teach the missing idea or show a worked example. Then ask the learner to apply it to a new case.

How is a hint different from giving the solution?+
A hint helps with the next decision while leaving meaningful work for the learner. For example, naming the relevant principle can help a student choose an operation without supplying every step and the final result.

# Flipped classrooms with AI tutoring: a lesson plan | Tutezy

# Flipped classrooms with AI tutoring: a lesson plan
In a flipped classroom, students encounter selected material before class and use class time to apply it with teacher support. An AI tutor can make preparation more interactive by asking questions and responding to confusion. The lesson still needs a clear connection between preparation, classroom activities and follow-up.
By the Tutezy team · October 10, 2026 · 5 min read

Key takeaways

- ✦ Flip one topic first and keep the preparation task short and focused.
- ✦ Collect evidence of understanding before deciding how to use class time.
- ✦ Provide an accessible catch-up route for students who could not prepare.
- ✦ Measure independent learning and staff workload, not just preparation completion.
In this article

- What changes in a flipped lesson
- Before class: purposeful preparation
- A 50-minute classroom plan
- After class: targeted follow-up
- Evaluate the first unit

## What changes when you flip a lesson?
The main change is how you use shared teaching time. If students encounter a basic explanation beforehand, class can focus on interpreting cases, comparing methods and resolving difficulties. If class simply repeats the preparation, students have little reason to invest in it next time.
Van Alten and colleagues’ 2019 meta-analysis examined 114 studies comparing flipped and non-flipped classrooms in secondary and postsecondary education. It found a small positive effect on learning outcomes, with substantial variation, and no overall effect on satisfaction. Designs retaining face-to-face time and including quizzes showed stronger learning outcomes. These findings are not a direct evaluation of AI tutoring.
A useful first experiment is one topic taught by a teacher who can review the preparation results. Keep the learning objective and assessment clear. Do not redesign a whole semester before seeing how students manage the new routine.

## Before class: give preparation a concrete purpose
Suppose the class will interpret a straight-line relationship using a fixed charge plus a variable charge. Before class, provide one worked example: a bike hire service charges $5 plus $2 per hour, represented by C = 5 + 2h. Explain the symbols and ask the student to calculate the cost for three hours: $11.
Then ask two questions: “What does the 5 represent?” and “How much does the cost change for one additional hour?” These responses provide more useful preparation evidence than whether the lesson was opened. Add a prompt asking what remains unclear.

- State what students should be able to do at the next class.
- Give an approximate time budget and a clear stopping point.
- Provide a readable version of the key explanation alongside any audio or video.
- Explain how to seek help and how the responses will be used.
- Review the answers early enough to adjust the classroom activity.
An AI tutor can ask the checks within a prepared lesson and respond to a mistaken interpretation. Keep the scope limited to the concept needed in class. A long detour into every related topic can leave students tired before the collaborative work begins.

## A sample 50-minute classroom plan
This timetable is an example to adapt to your class. The central activity compares two hire plans: Plan A costs $5 plus $2 per hour, while Plan B costs $1 plus $3 per hour. They cost the same at four hours, when each costs $13.
Time | Activity | Teacher’s decision |

0–5 minutes | Independent entry question on fixed and variable charges. | Check whether the preparation evidence matches current understanding. |
5–12 minutes | Brief worked recap for those who need it; an extension prompt for others. | Address the most common prerequisite gap. |
12–27 minutes | Pairs compare both plans using a table, graph or equation. | Ask students to explain why their representation is useful. |
27–40 minutes | Groups discuss which plan is cheaper for different durations. | Bring out the crossover point and the meaning of slope. |
40–47 minutes | Each student solves a fresh comparison independently. | Separate individual understanding from group success. |
47–50 minutes | Exit ticket: explain one decision and name one remaining question. | Choose the follow-up task. |

Have pairs justify their recommendations for two hours and six hours. Plan B is cheaper for two hours ($7 versus $9), while Plan A is cheaper for six ($17 versus $19). This makes the interpretation matter, rather than treating the intersection as an isolated calculation.
Plan for incomplete preparation
Offer the same core explanation in a short catch-up task. Find out whether students lacked access or misunderstood the task. Keep a route into the group activity so a missed preparation session does not become a missed classroom lesson too.

## After class: assign the next useful task
Use the independent work to select follow-up. A student who can calculate costs but cannot explain the fixed charge needs a different activity from one who understands the model but makes arithmetic errors. A student who can do both can compare a new situation with a different crossover point.
Keep the follow-up brief and state its purpose. Add a later question on the same idea to the next lesson. Our spaced revision plan shows how to revisit material without assigning the entire lesson again.

## Evaluate the first flipped unit
Collect three kinds of information: whether students could access and complete preparation, whether they learned the target concept independently, and whether the routine was manageable for staff. Record time spent preparing materials and reviewing responses. More interaction is useful only if it supports the learning objective.
Compare fresh assessment tasks with earlier work of similar difficulty, while acknowledging differences in students and teaching time. Ask learners which preparation prompts helped them enter the classroom activity. Revise one part of the sequence before extending the model to another unit.
Where Tutezy fits

## What we built for this
Tutezy can turn your existing lesson material into live individual lessons with checks and hints. That can support the preparation or follow-up portion of a flipped course. Explore Tutezy for universities or course creators , and review the reporting workflow during a demo.

## Sources

- Van Alten et al., Effects of flipping the classroom on learning outcomes and satisfaction: A meta-analysis (2019). doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2019.05.003

## Frequently asked questions
What is a flipped classroom?+
A flipped classroom moves selected initial learning before the class meeting and uses classroom time for application, discussion and feedback. It requires planning both parts together, rather than simply assigning a video as homework.

How can AI tutoring support a flipped classroom?+
A tutor can guide a prepared lesson, ask students to explain ideas and provide hints before class. Teachers can then use evidence of confusion to plan classroom activities. Confirm how the platform makes that information available.

What if students do not complete the preparation?+
Provide a short catch-up activity or a supported preparation period. Check whether access, time, unclear instructions or difficult content caused the problem before changing the workload or drawing conclusions about motivation.

# Spaced repetition: a practical four-week study plan | Tutezy

Exam prep

# Spaced repetition: a practical four-week study plan
Spaced repetition means revisiting material across separate study sessions. Combine it with retrieval practice: try to recall, explain or solve before checking the answer. A useful revision plan includes corrective feedback, room for difficult topics and fresh questions that test more than recognition.
By the Tutezy team · October 10, 2026 · 5 min read

Key takeaways

- ✦ Spread revision across days and weeks instead of concentrating it in one sitting.
- ✦ Retrieve first, then check the answer and correct the reasoning.
- ✦ Use calculations and explanations alongside flashcards.
- ✦ Adjust the next review using independent performance, not familiarity.
In this article

- Spacing and retrieval are different
- A four-week revision schedule
- Choose the right practice task
- Keep a useful error log
- Use an AI tutor for revision

## Spaced repetition and retrieval practice are different choices
Spacing describes when you revisit material. Retrieval describes what you do when you revisit it. Reading a page on Monday and again on Thursday is spaced study, but it does not require the same effort as closing the page and explaining the idea from memory.
The IES practice guide recommends spacing learning over time and using quizzes to revisit key content. Our schedule below applies those broad principles; its exact dates are an illustrative planning choice, not a uniquely validated formula.
For an educator, this distinction changes the assignment. “Review chapter three” leaves the task unclear. “Without notes, solve one question on each of these two methods, check your reasoning and record the mistake you need to revisit” produces evidence the learner and teacher can use.

## A practical four-week revision schedule
Choose a small set of objectives from material that has already been taught. For a first cycle, that might be rearranging a linear equation, interpreting a straight-line graph and explaining the meaning of its slope. Keep the sessions short enough to fit alongside current coursework.
When | What to do | What to record |

Day 1 | Review the original explanation, then attempt a short question without notes. | Starting understanding and any prerequisite gaps. |
Day 3 | Recall the key idea and solve a new example before checking. | Whether the answer was independent or needed a hint. |
Day 7 | Return to the topic with a different representation or context. | Which mistakes recur after a gap. |
Day 14 | Mix the topic with another previously taught skill. | Whether the learner chooses the right method without being told. |
Day 21 | Attempt a short application task and explain the reasoning. | Success on a question that differs from the original example. |
Day 28 | Complete a cumulative independent check. | What can be reviewed less often and what still needs teaching. |

Adapt the dates when the evidence changes. If a learner cannot begin a problem on Day 3, revisit the explanation and prerequisite before waiting until Day 7. If the idea remains secure over several checks, use less frequent maintenance practice. A missed session should lead to a manageable restart, not a doubled workload that crowds out new learning.
For several subjects, stagger the starting dates. Build a calendar from realistic available study time, then choose the most important objectives that fit. Adding every detail from every chapter can produce an unmanageable review queue.

## Choose a retrieval task that matches the objective

### Facts and vocabulary
Use a question on the front of a card and a checked answer on the back. For example, ask for the meaning of “denominator” before revealing it. Add an example requiring the learner to identify the denominator in a fraction so the task tests use as well as wording.

### Calculations and procedures
Solve a complete problem with the answer hidden. For 4x + 7 = 23, the learner should subtract 7 from both sides, divide by 4 and verify x = 4 in the original equation. On a later day, change the structure or context and ask which operation should come first.

### Explanations and diagrams
Ask the learner to sketch and label a process from memory, explain why a graph changes or predict an outcome under stated conditions. Compare the response with a short rubric of essential ideas. Exact wording should not be required where several explanations are valid.
A familiar answer can hide a weak concept
If the student remembers the answer because the same question has appeared repeatedly, introduce a fresh example. Keep the principle consistent while changing the numbers, representation or situation.

## Keep an error log that changes the next session
A useful log has four fields: the concept, what went wrong, the correction and the next check. For example: “Distributing a multiplier; multiplied only the first term; multiply every term inside the brackets; expand a new expression independently next session.”
Distinguish a reading slip from an insecure concept. If the student can explain and correct a slip immediately, one fresh check may be enough. If the same misconception recurs, schedule a teaching activity before more retrieval practice. Repeatedly testing an idea the learner has never understood is unlikely to resolve the underlying confusion.
Keep the log selective. Record recurring or consequential errors rather than copying every wrong answer. For a class, use patterns across the logs to decide which concepts need a shared explanation and which need individual support.

## Use an AI tutor for explanation and follow-up
An AI tutor can guide a review lesson, ask an explanation question and provide a hint when a learner is stuck. Keep at least one task outside the supported exchange so you can distinguish learning from successful prompting. Validate generated practice questions and answer keys before assigning them.
Keep the calendar in a tool you already use unless the tutoring product has a verified scheduling feature. Revisiting a weak concept within a lesson is different from automatically scheduling reviews over several weeks. Confirm which behavior is supported before promising it to students.
For exam providers, connect the revision cycle to your reviewed course objectives and approved practice bank. Our certification exam tutoring guide covers planning targeted support after mock tests.
Where Tutezy fits

## What we built for this
Tutezy checks concepts, revisits weak areas and opens subsequent lessons with a recap. Educators can combine that lesson support with their own revision calendar and independent assessments. Explore Tutezy for coaching institutes or independent tutors .

## Sources

- IES, Organizing Instruction and Study to Improve Student Learning (2007), spacing and quizzing recommendations. ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/PracticeGuide/1

## Frequently asked questions
What is spaced repetition?+
Spaced repetition is revisiting learned material across separated study sessions. It can involve recall questions, explanations, flashcards or problem solving. The schedule should fit the material, the learner and the date when the knowledge will be needed.

Is there a best spaced repetition schedule?+
There is no single timetable that is best for every subject and learner. Use a manageable starting schedule, check independent recall and bring difficult material back sooner. Extend gaps when performance remains secure.

Does spaced repetition work for math revision?+
You can space math practice by returning to previously taught problem types across sessions. Include complete problems, explanations and method selection, not only cards containing formulas. Check solutions after an attempt and revisit the cause of errors.

# Bloom's 2 sigma problem: can AI tutoring close the gap? | Tutezy
URL: https://tutezy.ai/blog/blooms-2-sigma-problem-ai-tutoring/

- Home
- ›
- Blog
- ›
- Learning science
Learning science

# Bloom's 2 sigma problem: can AI tutoring close the gap?
Bloom’s 2 sigma problem comes from a 1984 paper in which Benjamin Bloom reported that students taught one to one, with regular checks and corrective work, scored about two standard deviations above students in a conventional class of 30: the average tutored student beat 98% of that class. The “problem” was getting that result without a tutor for every student. Larger studies since then put typical tutoring gains at roughly 0.2 to 0.8 standard deviations, and the first generative-AI trials show that the tutor’s design decides whether AI helps or hurts learning.
By the Tutezy team · September 25, 2026 · 13 min read

Key takeaways

- ✦ The 2 sigma number is real but narrow. It came from two University of Chicago dissertations: three-week units in probability and cartography, measured with tests written for those units.
- ✦ About half the effect was mastery learning. Regular checks plus corrective work, with no tutor, moved the average student from the 50th to about the 84th percentile.
- ✦ Typical tutoring effects are smaller, and still large. VanLehn’s 2011 review found 0.79 SD for human tutors; a 2024 meta-analysis of randomized tutoring experiments found 0.288 SD.
- ✦ AI tutoring can go either way. A structured AI tutor at Harvard more than doubled median gains in two physics lessons; open GPT-4 access in a Turkish high school left students 17% worse once it was taken away.
- ✦ Design for the mechanism, not the chat. Teach a plan, check after each concept, hint before telling, hold off moving on until it is understood, and come back to what was weak.
In this article

- What Bloom’s paper actually found
- What “2 sigma” means in percentiles
- Why later research shrank the number
- What AI tutoring trials have found
- The mechanisms behind the effect
- What this means for AI tutor design
- Is it still a cost problem?
- How to read an AI tutoring claim

## What did Bloom’s 2 sigma paper actually find?
In the June–July 1984 issue of Educational Researcher, Benjamin Bloom, then at the University of Chicago and Northwestern University, published “The 2 Sigma Problem: The Search for Methods of Group Instruction as Effective as One-to-One Tutoring.” The headline result did not come from a large trial. It came from dissertations by two of his doctoral students, Joanne Anania and Joseph Burke, which compared three ways of teaching the same material:

- Conventional: about 30 students per teacher, with periodic tests used for grades.
- Mastery learning: the same class size and usually the same teacher, plus formative tests used for feedback, corrective work for students who had not yet mastered the unit, and a parallel test to check that they now had.
- Tutoring: a good tutor for each student (or for two or three at once), followed by the same cycle of formative tests, feedback and correctives.
Students were randomly assigned to the three conditions. Bloom reports that the study was replicated with four samples of students in grades 4, 5 and 8, in two subjects (probability and cartography), with instruction limited to 11 class periods over three weeks.
The results were striking. Measured in standard deviations (sigma) of the conventional class, the average tutored student scored about 2 sigma higher: above 98% of the control class. The average mastery-learning student scored about 1 sigma higher: above 84%. Around 90% of tutored students and 70% of mastery-learning students reached the level that only the top 20% of the conventional class reached. Time on task moved the same way, from about 65% in conventional classes to 75% under mastery learning and over 90% under tutoring.
The “problem” in the title was economic. Bloom called one-to-one tutoring “too costly for most societies to bear on a large scale” and asked researchers to find group methods that could match it. Most of the paper is about that search: pairing mastery learning with other changes, such as better explanations or more student participation, to see whether two changes together could approach 2 sigma.

## What does “2 sigma” mean in percentiles?
A sigma is one standard deviation of the comparison group’s scores. If scores are roughly normal, a student at the average sits at the 50th percentile, one standard deviation above sits at about the 84th, and two above sits at about the 98th. That is the arithmetic behind Bloom’s two claims.
Conventional class (1 : 30)Mastery learning (1 : 30)Tutoring (1 : 1)
-
-
- 50th84th98th← percentile of theconventional class
-
- −2
- −1
- 0
- +1
- +2
- +3
- +4Final test score, in standard deviations of the conventional class
Schematic of Bloom’s 1984 comparison, with scores in standard deviations of the conventional class. The mastery-learning average sits 1 SD above the conventional average (84th percentile); the tutoring average sits 2 SD above (98th). All three curves are drawn with the same spread for clarity; in Bloom’s data the mastery and tutoring groups were also less spread out.In classroom terms: in a conventional class of 30, a 2 sigma gain means the typical tutored student would outscore about 29 of them. Smaller effects still matter. A gain of 0.3 SD moves an average student from the 50th to about the 62nd percentile; 0.8 SD moves them to about the 79th. Keep those conversions in mind for the numbers that follow.

## Why did later research shrink the 2 sigma effect?
Bloom’s number has become shorthand for what tutoring can do, but it does not describe what tutoring typically does. Four things explain the gap.
The tests were narrow. Anania and Burke chose probability and cartography because the topics were unfamiliar to the students, and the post-test covered exactly what the three-week unit taught. In a 2024 essay in Education Next, Paul von Hippel points to a 1982 meta-analysis by Cohen, Kulik and Kulik that found tutoring effects averaged 0.84 SD on narrow tests written by the researchers, but only 0.27 SD on broader standardized tests.
Half the effect was mastery learning. The mastery-learning classes, with no tutor, gained about 1 SD on their own (von Hippel puts it at about 1.1). The tutoring condition included the same formative tests and correctives. So 2 sigma is the result of tutoring plus regular checks and corrections, not of a tutor alone.
Reviews of many studies found smaller effects. Kurt VanLehn’s 2011 review in Educational Psychologist compared human tutoring, computer tutoring and no tutoring. It noted the common belief that adult human tutors produce an effect of about 2.0, and found d = 0.79 instead. Intelligent tutoring systems, most of which work step by step, came in at 0.76, “nearly as effective as human tutoring.” A 2024 meta-analysis of randomized preK–12 tutoring experiments by Nickow, Oreopoulos and Quan in the American Educational Research Journal found a pooled effect of 0.288 SD. Effects were largest for programs that used teachers or paraprofessionals as tutors, ran in earlier grades, met at least three days a week and took place during the school day.
Scale adds friction. High-dosage tutoring works at scale, but at a different size. Two randomized trials of Saga Education’s math tutoring for secondary students in Chicago, published by Guryan and colleagues in the American Economic Review in 2023, found gains of 0.18 to 0.40 SD in math test scores that persisted into later years. The program used paraprofessional tutors to hold down cost.
Is 0.3 SD a disappointment?
No. Nickow and colleagues describe their pooled result as “consistently substantial,” and it came from randomized experiments on real school programs. The error is expecting 2.0 because a 1984 paper reported it for a three-week unit test. When anyone quotes Bloom to sell you something, ask what kind of test their own number came from.

## What have AI tutoring trials found so far?
Generative AI revived the 2 sigma question, because an AI tutor costs a fraction of a human one. Three studies published in 2025 are worth knowing in detail, because they point in different directions.
Study | Setting | What students used | Result |

Kestin et al., Scientific Reports (2025) | Harvard undergraduate physics course, 194 students, two lessons, each student tried both conditions | A custom GPT-4 tutor with step-by-step solutions written into its prompts, used at home, vs an in-class active-learning lesson | Median learning gains more than double the class; estimated effect 0.73–1.3 SD; median 49 minutes vs a 60-minute class |
De Simone et al., World Bank (2025) | Nigeria, six-week after-school program for first-year senior secondary students, June–July 2024 | Microsoft Copilot (GPT-4) twice a week, with teachers guiding students and suggesting prompts | 0.31 SD on the overall assessment; 0.23 SD on English, the main outcome |
Bastani et al., PNAS (2025) | High school in Turkey, nearly 1,000 students, four 90-minute math sessions | “GPT Base” (a ChatGPT-style interface) or “GPT Tutor” (prompts built around teacher-designed hints) | Practice grades up 48% (Base) and 127% (Tutor); on a later exam without AI, Base students scored 17% lower than controls; Tutor largely avoided the harm |

The Harvard result is the one most often quoted as “AI reaches 2 sigma.” It does not quite say that. The comparison was a strong active-learning class, not a lecture; it covered two lessons, surface tension and fluid flow; and the post-test came right after each lesson. The authors also note that the tutor’s accuracy relied on pre-written answers. It is still the best evidence so far that a carefully structured AI tutor can teach a lesson well, in less time.
The Nigeria pilot matters because it ran in real schools as an after-school program. The World Bank team equates the gain to 1.5 to 2 years of “business-as-usual” schooling and reports that students who attended more sessions gained more. Teachers were in the room, opening each session with a suggested prompt and guiding students as they worked.
The Turkish study is the warning. Students with open GPT-4 access used it as a crutch: they did better while it was there and worse once it was gone. The version that gave teacher-designed hints instead of answers largely avoided the drop. Same model, opposite effect on learning. The difference was design.

## What made tutoring work in the first place?
Strip Bloom’s tutoring condition and the newer studies down to what the tutor actually did, and the same mechanisms keep appearing. None of them is “a smarter explanation.”

- Frequent checks. Formative tests after each unit in Bloom’s studies; in one-to-one teaching, the check can come after every step. The teacher finds out what the student understood instead of assuming it. Our guide to checking for understanding covers twelve ways to do this online.
- Correctives, then a second check. Mastery learning did not just return a score. Students who had not mastered the unit did corrective work and then took a parallel test.
- Mastery before moving on. The next unit built on a foundation the student had shown, not one the schedule assumed.
- The student does the thinking. Time on task passed 90% under tutoring. In the Turkish study, the tutor that withheld answers protected learning; the one that handed them out did not.
- Accurate, timely feedback at the student’s pace. Kestin and colleagues list scaffolding, managing cognitive load, accurate feedback delivered promptly and self-pacing among the practices their AI tutor was designed around. Their students’ time on the lesson varied widely and did not predict their post-test score.

## What does this mean for how an AI tutor should be designed?
The evidence adds up to a fairly concrete specification. An AI tutor meant to capture some of the tutoring effect should do six things:

- 1 Teach from a plan
A sequence of concepts taken from the course, taught in order. A blank chat box assumes the student already knows what to ask.

- 2 Check after each concept
A question whose answer shows understanding, scored against a rubric. “Does that make sense?” is not a check.

- 3 Hint before telling
Give the smallest nudge that lets the student find the answer. Handing over answers is the GPT Base condition.

- 4 Hold the line on mastery, with a cap
Don’t advance on a wrong answer, but cap the retries and flag the student for a human rather than looping forever.

- 5 Revisit what was weak
Come back to shaky concepts before the topic closes and at the start of the next session, instead of trusting one right answer.

- 6 Stay anchored to vetted material
The Harvard tutor’s accuracy relied on solutions written by instructors. Grounding the tutor in reviewed content does the same job.

A general chatbot does the opposite by default: it waits to be asked, answers in full and never learns whether the student understood. That is not a flaw in the model, it is a mismatch of job. We compare the two approaches on Tutezy vs ChatGPT , and cover how grounding keeps a tutor faithful to your material in keeping an AI tutor grounded .

## Is the 2 sigma problem still a cost problem?
Bloom framed his problem in terms of cost, so it is worth doing the sum. In the Chicago trials reported by Guryan and colleagues, Saga’s program gave students 50 minutes of tutoring every school day, two students per tutor, and cost $3,200 to $4,800 per student per year during the study. The authors compare that with Chicago Public Schools’ spending of about $17,000 per pupil. That is cheap for human tutoring, and still a large new line in any school or course budget.
Per-minute AI pricing changes the arithmetic. At $0.03 a learner-minute (Tutezy’s rate; other tools charge per seat or per student, compared in how much an AI tutor costs ), the same 50 minutes a day is $1.50. Over an assumed 180-day school year, that is $270 per student. The catch is that the price is the only part of the comparison anyone knows. None of the studies above tested an AI tutor at that dose for a full year, so nobody should promise Saga’s 0.18 to 0.40 SD from one, and the Turkish study shows how easily an AI tutor can produce a loss. The budget side of Bloom’s problem has become easy. The design and evidence sides have not.

## How should you read an AI tutoring claim?
Any vendor, including us, will be tempted to quote Bloom. Before you believe a sigma number attached to a product, ask these questions:

- What was the test? A test written for the unit just taught will show a much bigger effect than a standardized test. Cohen, Kulik and Kulik’s 0.84 vs 0.27 is the size of that difference.
- How long was the study? Two lessons, three weeks and a school year are different claims.
- What was the comparison? Nothing, a lecture, or a strong active-learning class?
- Was learning measured without the AI? Scores while the tool is available can rise even when learning falls.
- Who were the learners, and who ran the study? Results from motivated volunteers or a vendor’s own analysis need independent replication.
For a buyer, the practical version is simpler: pilot on one chapter, give a short quiz a week later without the tutor, and compare it with a group that studied the usual way. Our buyer’s checklist for AI tutoring software walks through setting that up.
Where Tutezy fits

## What we built for this
Tutezy is built around the parts of the tutoring recipe that software can carry. Each chapter of an institute’s own PDFs, slides or videos is compiled into a teaching plan of concepts, checks, hints and common misconceptions, which the institute reviews before students see it. The live lesson teaches that plan one to one on a whiteboard, asks a question after each concept, scores the voice or typed answer against a rubric, gives a hint before the answer, caps remediation loops, revisits weak concepts before moving on and recaps them at the start of the next lesson. Teachers see concept mastery per student and weak spots per batch. The mechanics are on how it works ; a lesson costs $0.03 per learner-minute (pricing ).
What it is not: a measured 2 sigma. The studies above describe what well-designed tutoring can do; they are not results for Tutezy, and we do not quote an effect size for it. It does not replace a human tutor’s judgment or relationship with a student, which is why it reports to one (Tutezy vs human tutoring ). And it teaches only what is in your material.

## Frequently asked questions
What is Bloom’s 2 sigma problem?+
In a 1984 paper in Educational Researcher, Benjamin Bloom reported that students tutored one to one, with regular checks and corrective work, scored about two standard deviations above students in a conventional class of about 30. The “problem” was that a tutor for every student is too expensive, so Bloom asked researchers to find group teaching methods that could get the same result.

Is the 2 sigma effect real?+
It was a real result in the studies Bloom described, but those were three-week units in probability and cartography, measured with tests written for that unit. Larger reviews find smaller effects: VanLehn’s 2011 review put human tutoring at 0.79 standard deviations, and a 2024 meta-analysis of randomized preK–12 tutoring experiments found a pooled effect of 0.288. Tutoring clearly works; 2 sigma is not what it typically delivers.

What does 2 sigma mean in percentiles?+
Sigma is one standard deviation of the comparison group’s scores. If scores are roughly normal, a student one standard deviation above the average sits at about the 84th percentile, and two above sits at about the 98th. That is why Bloom wrote that the average tutored student was above 98% of the students in the conventional class.

What is the effect size of one-to-one tutoring?+
It depends on the study and the test. Kurt VanLehn’s 2011 review found d = 0.79 for human tutoring, and a 2024 meta-analysis by Nickow, Oreopoulos and Quan found a pooled 0.288 SD across randomized tutoring experiments, with larger effects for teacher or paraprofessional tutors, earlier grades and sessions at least three days a week. Effects measured on narrow tests written by researchers tend to be much larger than effects on standardized tests.

Can AI tutoring close the 2 sigma gap?+
Not proven. A 2025 Harvard physics trial found a structured AI tutor more than doubled median learning gains over an active-learning class across two lessons, with an estimated effect of 0.73 to 1.3 standard deviations. A 2025 study in a Turkish high school found that unguarded GPT-4 access left students 17% worse on a later exam taken without it. The design of the tutor decides which result you get.

Does using ChatGPT help students learn?+
Used as an answer machine, it can hurt. In the Bastani et al. study published in PNAS in 2025, students with a ChatGPT-style interface did better during practice but 17% worse than a control group once access was removed. A version that gave teacher-designed hints instead of answers largely avoided that harm.

# Checking for understanding: 12 techniques that work online | Tutezy
URL: https://tutezy.ai/blog/checking-for-understanding-techniques/

- Blog
- ›
