Learning science

# Checking for understanding: 12 techniques that work online
Checking for understanding means getting evidence of what each learner actually understood before you move on, instead of asking “Any questions?” and treating silence as a yes. The checking for understanding strategies that work online all make the learner produce something you can read: an answer to a question whose wrong options map to misconceptions, a prediction, an explanation in their own words, a worked step. Below are 12 techniques, each with an online example, the common pitfall and how an AI tutor can run it.
By the Tutezy team · September 25, 2026 · 13 min read

Key takeaways

- ✦ Silence is not evidence. “Any questions?” and “Does that make sense?” check confidence, and learners are poor judges of their own understanding.
- ✦ Every learner answers, every time. A check that only volunteers respond to tells you about the volunteers.
- ✦ Design the wrong answers. A hinge question whose distractors match known misconceptions tells you what to reteach, not just who got it wrong.
- ✦ Check again later. A low-stakes quiz after a delay beats rereading for long-term recall; in one classic study, 61% vs 40% after a week.
- ✦ A check is only useful if it changes what happens next. Hint, reteach, move on or come back later: decide before you ask.
In this article

- Why “Any questions?” fails
- What the research says
- Checks while you teach (1–4)
- Checks after a concept (5–8)
- Checks that come back later (9–12)
- All 12 techniques at a glance
- A 15-minute lesson with checks built in

## Why don’t “Any questions?” and “Does that make sense?” work?
Checking for understanding is the habit of collecting evidence, during the lesson, of what each learner has actually understood. The two most common checks collect almost none. “Any questions?” asks a learner to diagnose their own confusion and admit it out loud. The ones who are most lost often cannot say what they don’t know. Online, with cameras off and a quiet chat, silence tells you even less.
“Does that make sense?” is worse, because it invites a yes. Learners mistake familiarity for understanding. In Roediger and Karpicke’s 2006 study in Psychological Science, students who spent four study periods rereading a passage were more confident they would remember it than students who read it once and then took three recall tests. A week later, the rereaders recalled 40% of the passage and the recall group 61%.
Black and Wiliam, reviewing classroom practice in 1998, described a related trap: a teacher who answers their own question after two or three seconds leaves no time to think, so questions drift toward the simple and the “discussion” happens with the few quick students. The fix is the same in both cases. Ask a question whose answer shows the understanding, and get an answer from every learner.
Three swaps to make today
“Any questions?” becomes “Which of these four answers is right, and why?”
“Does that make sense?” becomes “In one sentence, why does a plant need light?”
“Got it?” becomes “Before I show you, predict what happens if we move the lamp away.”

## What does the research say about checking for understanding?
The case for checking rests on two bodies of evidence. The first is formative assessment. Black and Wiliam’s 1998 review, summarized for teachers as “Inside the Black Box,” reported effect sizes of 0.4 to 0.7 in the formative-assessment studies it reviewed. Later work was more cautious. A 2011 meta-analysis by Kingston and Nash reviewed more than 300 studies, found only 13 with enough information to calculate effects, and estimated a weighted mean effect of 0.20, higher in English language arts (0.32) than in math (0.17) or science (0.09). Computer-based formative systems came in at 0.28. The honest reading: checking helps, and how much depends on what you do with the answer.
The second is cognitive science on how people remember. Dunlosky and colleagues’ 2013 review of ten study techniques rated practice testing and distributed practice as high utility, self-explanation as moderate, and rereading and highlighting as low. Several of the techniques below are checks and learning events at once: answering the question is itself part of how the idea sticks.

## Checks while you teach (techniques 1–4)
The examples use one topic throughout, a first lesson on photosynthesis, so you can see how the checks fit together.

### 1. Hinge questions with misconception-mapped options
A multiple-choice question asked at the point where your next move depends on the answer. Dylan Wiliam’s rule of thumb: students should need no more than two minutes to answer, and you should be able to read every response in 30 seconds or less. The aim is that students with the right thinking and students with the wrong thinking give different answers.
Example: “Most of the dry mass of a large tree comes from: (A) minerals in the soil, (B) water, (C) carbon dioxide from the air, (D) sunlight.” The answer is C; A, B and D each match a common misconception. Pitfall: distractors nobody would pick, which make the question a formality. AI tutor: store the misconception behind each wrong option in the lesson plan, so a wrong choice triggers the hint written for that mistake.

### 2. Predict, then reveal
Ask for a prediction before showing the result, then ask the learner to explain any gap. Science teachers know it as predict–observe–explain, described by White and Gunstone in Probing Understanding.
Example: “A plant is sealed in a jar in the dark for two days. Will the carbon dioxide in the jar go up, down or stay the same?” (Up: respiration continues, photosynthesis stops.) Pitfall: revealing the answer without asking why the prediction was off, which is where the learning happens. AI tutor: record the prediction, show the result on the board, then ask for the explanation and score it.

### 3. Explain it back
The learner explains the idea in their own words. In Chi and colleagues’ 1994 study, eighth graders who were simply prompted to explain each line of a text on the circulatory system to themselves gained more from pretest to posttest than a control group who read it twice. It was a small study (14 prompted students, 10 controls); Dunlosky’s review, looking across the wider research, rates self-explanation as moderately useful.
Example: “In one sentence, why does a plant need light to make glucose?” A good answer says light supplies the energy and that energy ends up stored in glucose. Pitfall: accepting a parroted phrase (“because of photosynthesis”). AI tutor: score the answer against a short rubric of must-have ideas and ask a follow-up about whichever one is missing.

### 4. No-opt-out follow-ups
When a learner says “I don’t know,” the exchange isn’t finished until that same learner gives the right answer. Doug Lemov named this “No Opt Out” in Teach Like a Champion.
Example: The learner can’t name the gas plants take in. Narrow it: “We breathe it out. What is it?” Then return to the original question and have them answer it in full. Pitfall: moving on to someone else, which teaches that “I don’t know” ends the question. AI tutor: nudge after silence, give a smaller hint, then re-ask the original question.

## Checks after a concept (techniques 5–8)

### 5. Find the error
Show a plausible answer containing one planted mistake and ask the learner to find and fix it. It tests whether they can apply the idea, not just recognize it.
Example: “A student writes: ‘Plants photosynthesize during the day and respire at night.’ What’s wrong?” (Plants respire all the time; in daylight, photosynthesis usually outpaces it.) Pitfall: leaving the wrong version as the last thing on screen. AI tutor: check that the learner both spots the error and states the corrected version, then write the correction on the board.

### 6. Confidence ratings
After answering, the learner rates their confidence: guessing, fairly sure or certain. Confidence alone is not evidence, as the rereading result above shows, but paired with the answer it sorts learners usefully. Confident and wrong is a misconception to fix first; unsure and right needs practice, not reteaching.
Example: after the tree-mass question, “How sure were you?” Pitfall: asking for confidence instead of an answer. AI tutor: store the rating with the answer and put confident-wrong concepts first in the revisit queue.

### 7. Apply it to a new case
Change the surface of the problem and keep the principle. A learner who has only memorized the example will stall.
Example: “Pondweed under a lamp gives off bubbles. What happens to the bubbles if you move the lamp farther away, and why?” (Fewer bubbles: less light, slower photosynthesis, less oxygen.) Pitfall: a “new” case that is the same example with new numbers. AI tutor: keep transfer questions and their expected answers in the reviewed lesson plan rather than improvising them, so the science stays right.

### 8. Show your work
Ask for the steps, not just the result. In a live online class, everyone writes on a shared whiteboard, or types in the chat and hits enter at the same moment so nobody copies.
Example: “Write the word equation for photosynthesis.” (Carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen, using light energy.) Pitfall: marking only the final line, which hides where the reasoning broke. AI tutor: ask for the steps one at a time by voice or text; handwritten working on paper is still easier for a human to read.

## Checks that come back later (techniques 9–12)

### 9. Exit tickets
Two or three quick prompts at the end of a lesson, read before the next one. Include one question on the hardest idea and one asking what is still unclear.
Example: “Name the two inputs of photosynthesis. Where in the cell does it happen? What’s one thing you’re unsure about?” Pitfall: collecting tickets nobody reads. AI tutor: turn the answers into a per-learner summary for the teacher and open the next session with the weakest point.

### 10. Low-stakes retrieval quizzes
Short recall questions, ungraded, with the answer given straight after. In Roediger and Karpicke’s experiment, rereading won on a test five minutes later (83% vs 71%), but after a week the recall group was well ahead (61% vs 40%).
Example: start the next session with “Without looking back: why did the bubbles slow down when the lamp moved?” Pitfall: treating it as a grade, which makes learners anxious and tempts them to look things up. AI tutor: ask aloud, score, give the answer, and log which ideas were forgotten.

### 11. Faded worked examples
Show a fully worked example, then remove steps one at a time until the learner does the whole problem. Renkl and Atkinson describe fading as a way to raise the demands gradually so learners aren’t overwhelmed; in “backward” fading, the last step is the first to go.
Example: worked: “45 bubbles in 3 minutes is 15 bubbles per minute.” Faded: “60 bubbles in 5 minutes. You do the last step.” Then: “Compare the rates at 20 cm and 40 cm from the lamp.” Pitfall: fading too fast, or never fading at all. AI tutor: ask for the next step before showing it on the board.

### 12. Spaced revisits of weak concepts
Come back to what was shaky after a gap: later in the lesson, at the start of the next one, a week on. Dunlosky’s review rates distributed practice as high utility.
Example: the learner missed the sealed-jar prediction, so revisit it at the end with a variant (the same jar in bright light) and again next session. Pitfall: revisiting everything equally, or straight away, which isn’t spacing. AI tutor: flag weak concepts per learner and schedule them into later recaps.

## All 12 checking for understanding strategies at a glance
Technique | Best moment | What it reveals | Pitfall to avoid |

1. Hinge question | Before building on a concept | Which misconception, per learner | Distractors nobody picks |
2. Predict, then reveal | Before a demo or result | The learner’s mental model | No “why” after the reveal |
3. Explain it back | Right after explaining | Whether the idea is in their words | Accepting parroted phrases |
4. No-opt-out follow-up | After “I don’t know” | Whether a hint is enough | Moving on to someone else |
5. Find the error | After a concept | Whether they can apply it | Wrong version left on screen |
6. Confidence rating | Paired with any answer | Confident-wrong misconceptions | Confidence instead of an answer |
7. Apply to a new case | End of a concept | Transfer beyond the example | Same example, new numbers |
8. Show your work | Multi-step problems | Where reasoning breaks | Marking only the final line |
9. Exit ticket | End of lesson | What to open the next lesson with | Nobody reads them |
10. Retrieval quiz | Start of next session | What was forgotten | Making it a grade |
11. Faded worked examples | Moving from examples to problems | Which step they can’t do alone | Fading too fast |
12. Spaced revisit | Later that lesson, next session | Whether a fix held | Revisiting everything, or too soon |

You don’t need all twelve in every lesson. A hinge question, an explain-it-back and a retrieval question next time cover most of the value. The rest are for when those show a problem.
If you are evaluating AI tools for any of this, the quickest test is whether the tool asks the learner questions or only answers them. A chatbot that explains well but never checks gives you the same false signal as “Does that make sense?” We compare the two designs in Tutezy vs ChatGPT .

## What does a 15-minute lesson with checks look like?
Here is how the photosynthesis lesson above might run one to one, online. Every step ends with the learner producing something, and every answer decides what happens next.

- 1 Warm-up retrieval (2 min)
Two recall questions on last lesson’s weakest point. Wrong answers get a quick reteach before anything new.

- 2 Inputs and outputs (4 min)
Teach the word equation, then the tree-mass hinge question. A wrong option triggers the hint for that misconception.

- 3 Why light matters (3 min)
Predict what happens when the lamp moves away, reveal, then “explain it back” in one sentence.

- 4 Measuring the rate (3 min)
A worked bubble-count example, then a faded one where the learner does the last step.

- 5 Find the error (2 min)
The “respire only at night” statement, with a confidence rating. Confident-wrong goes to the top of the revisit list.

- 6 Exit ticket (1 min)
Three prompts. Weak concepts become the next session’s warm-up, which closes the loop.

This is the same loop that made tutoring effective in the studies behind Bloom’s 2 sigma problem : check, correct, don’t build on a gap, come back to it. For self-paced courses, the same checks placed between videos are one of the fixes in our guide to improving online course completion rates .
Where Tutezy fits

## What we built for this
Tutezy runs several of these checks in every lesson without a teacher present. Each concept in a compiled lesson plan carries a check (multiple choice, short answer or predict-then-reveal) with an expected answer, a rubric, common misconceptions with hints, and a pass threshold. Students answer by voice or typing; a long silence gets a nudge. A wrong answer gets a hint first, then the answer kept on the board; remediation loops are capped. Worked examples ask for the next step before showing it. Weak concepts are revisited before the topic closes and recapped at the start of the next lesson, and teachers see concept mastery per student and weak spots per batch. The mechanism is on how it works ; schools can see the set-up on Tutezy for schools , and lessons cost $0.03 per learner-minute (pricing ).
Where it is not the right tool: checks that depend on reading a student’s handwritten working, or on a whole-class discussion, are still a human teacher’s job. The checks are compiled from your own material, so their quality depends on it, and the institute reviews them before students see them.

## Frequently asked questions
What does checking for understanding mean?+
Checking for understanding means collecting evidence of what each learner actually understood, during the lesson, so you can decide whether to move on, reteach or give a hint. It is the in-the-moment part of formative assessment. A good check makes every learner produce something you can read, such as an answer, a prediction or an explanation, rather than relying on who speaks up.

What are some checking for understanding strategies?+
Twelve that work online and one to one: hinge questions with misconception-based options, predict-then-reveal, explain it back, no-opt-out follow-ups, find the error, confidence ratings, apply it to a new case, show your work, exit tickets, low-stakes retrieval quizzes, faded worked examples and spaced revisits of weak concepts. Each one makes the learner’s thinking visible so you can act on it.

Why is “Does that make sense?” a bad question?+
It invites a yes, and learners are poor judges of their own understanding. In Roediger and Karpicke’s 2006 study, students who reread a passage felt more confident than students who practiced recalling it, yet recalled less a week later. Ask a question whose answer shows the understanding instead.

What is a hinge question?+
A hinge question is a quick multiple-choice question asked at the point where the lesson’s next step depends on the answer. Dylan Wiliam suggests students should need no more than two minutes to answer it and the teacher no more than 30 seconds to read the responses. Each wrong option should match a specific misconception, so the answer tells you what to reteach.

How do you check for understanding online?+
Make every learner respond, not just volunteers: polls or multiple-choice hinge questions, typed or spoken one-sentence explanations, predictions before a reveal, and short quizzes at the start of the next session. In one-to-one online teaching, ask a question after each new concept and do not move on until the answer shows the idea has landed.

How often should you check for understanding?+
Check whenever the next part of the lesson depends on the last one, which in one-to-one teaching usually means after each new concept. Then check again later: a quick retrieval question at the start of the next session catches what was forgotten, and revisiting weak concepts after a gap uses the spacing effect.

# How to improve online course completion rates | Tutezy
URL: https://tutezy.ai/blog/improve-online-course-completion-rates/

- Home
- ›
- Blog
- ›
- Course creators
Course creators

# How to improve online course completion rates
Online course completion rates are low by default: across Harvard and MIT courses on edX, 3.13% of all participants completed in 2017–18, and even among learners who paid for a certificate only 46% finished. To improve completion, make the course easier to keep doing (short units, a plan at the start, deadlines or a cohort), make every unit end with a question, and make sure a stuck learner can get unstuck the same day. Measure activation, unit-one completion and week-two retention, because those move long before the final completion rate does.
By the Tutezy team · September 25, 2026 · 12 min read

Key takeaways

- ✦ Low completion is normal. 3.13% of all edX participants at Harvard and MIT in 2017–18; a median of 12.6% across 221 MOOCs; 46% even for paying learners.
- ✦ The first two weeks decide most of it. In Jordan’s data, the share of active learners levels out after weeks one and two. Fix onboarding before the finale.
- ✦ Short units with questions. Median video engagement was at most 6 minutes, and quizzes between lecture segments cut mind-wandering from 41% to 19% in one experiment.
- ✦ Nudges help less at scale. Planning prompts raised completion 29% in three courses, but across 247 courses similar prompts lifted early engagement, not completion.
- ✦ Being stuck is the quiet exit. A learner who hits a concept they can’t get past, with nobody to ask, rarely emails you. They just stop.
In this article

- What completion rates look like
- Why learners drop out
- The metrics to track
- How to diagnose a stall point
- Fixes the research supports
- Deadlines, cohorts and reminders
- Where live help fits
- A 30-day plan

## What do online course completion rates actually look like?
Most people who enroll in an online course don’t finish it, and the best public data shows the rate hasn’t improved with time. The best public data comes from MOOCs, because researchers could see every learner. A 2019 analysis in Science by Justin Reich and José Ruipérez-Valiente covered every Harvard and MIT course on edX from 2012 to 2018: 5.63 million learners in 12.67 million course registrations. The results:
Group | Completion | Source |

All participants, Harvard and MIT edX courses, 2017–18 | 3.13%, down from nearly 6% in 2014–15 | Reich & Ruipérez-Valiente (2019) |
Learners who paid for a verified certificate, 2017–18 | 46%, down from 56% in 2016–17 | Reich & Ruipérez-Valiente (2019) |
221 MOOCs, share of enrolled students completing | Median 12.6% (range 0.7% to 52.1%) | Jordan (2015) |

Two lessons for a paid course creator. First, paying helps but doesn’t solve it: more than half of paying edX learners still didn’t finish. Second, published figures are only a rough frame. Katy Jordan’s study found completion fell as courses got longer, so a 12-week course and a 3-week one aren’t comparable. You will see much higher completion figures quoted for cohort-based or premium courses, usually self-reported by the vendor; treat those as marketing until you can see how “completion” and “enrolled” were defined. The benchmark that matters is your own last cohort.

## Why do learners drop out of online courses?
“No time” is the easy explanation. Look at where learners actually stop, though, and six causes come up again and again:

- No plan. Learners intend to finish, then never decide when. Yeomans and Reich call this the intention–action gap: among MOOC learners who intend to complete, the majority don’t.
- No accountability. Nobody notices if they miss a week, so missing a week costs nothing, and then it’s two.
- Passive, long video. Watching feels like progress but asks nothing of the learner, and long videos lose people partway through.
- Stuck on one concept. In a Spanish course, this is often the module on ser vs estar. The learner can’t get past it, the forum answer comes two days later, and by then they have stopped opening the app.
- Modules too long to finish in one sitting. A 45-minute module started at 10 pm is a module half-finished, and half-finished modules are where streaks end.
- Heavy work before the habit forms. Jordan found that courses graded only automatically had higher completion rates. One reading: a big peer-reviewed project in week one asks for commitment before the learner has any.
Only the first two are about motivation. The other four are design problems you can fix this month.

## Which metrics should you track to improve course completion?
Final completion is a lagging number: by the time it moves, the cohort is over. Track the leading ones instead. Jordan’s analysis of MOOC activity found the first and second weeks are critical, after which the share of active students levels out. So most of what you can change happens early.

- Activation: enrollees who start lesson one within 7 days ÷ all enrollees.
- Unit-one completion: learners who finish the first unit ÷ all enrollees.
- Week-two retention: learners active in days 8–14 ÷ learners who activated.
- Stall points: for each lesson, the share of learners who reach it but never finish it. The biggest numbers are your to-do list.
- Time to an answer: how long a question posted by a learner waits for a reply.
Here is what the funnel looks like for an illustrative 8-module Spanish course (made-up numbers, not a benchmark):
Stage | Learners | Share of enrolled |

Enrolled | 1,000 | 100% |
Started lesson 1 within 7 days (activation) | 640 | 64% |
Finished unit 1 | 450 | 45% |
Active in week 2 | 330 | 33% |
Reached module 4 (ser vs estar) | 240 | 24% |
Finished module 4 | 150 | 15% |
Completed the course | 120 | 12% |

Read it from the top. 360 people never started, which is an onboarding problem. Week-two retention is 330 ÷ 640, about 52%. Module 4 loses 90 of the 240 who reach it, a stall point of 37.5%, far worse than the modules after it. That is where a better explanation, practice questions or live help would pay off first.

## How do you diagnose a stall point?
A drop in the funnel tells you where learners leave, not why. The pattern around it usually does. Match what you see to the likely cause before you change anything:
What you see | Likely cause | First fix |

Many enroll, few start lesson 1 | Onboarding friction, no plan | A short first lesson with a quick win, a planning prompt, a resume email on day 2 |
Viewers leave partway through the same long video | Too long or too dense | Split it into segments under about 6 minutes with questions between them |
A drop at one module, with more questions or rewatches there | A hard concept, explained once | A second explanation, worked examples, practice questions and a way to ask |
Steady decline week after week | No accountability | Cohort start dates, soft deadlines, weekly progress notes |
A drop at the first big assignment | Too heavy or unclear | A smaller first task with a model answer, and practice before the graded piece |
Learners finish but fail the final quiz | Watching without checking | Questions in every unit, and a revisit of weak topics before the final |

In the Spanish example, module 4 fits the third row. Ser vs estar is one idea with a lot of exceptions, and one video rarely lands it for everyone. A short contrast table, ten quick “ser or estar?” questions with instant feedback, and somewhere to ask when a sentence doesn’t seem to fit the rule will do more than re-recording the video in better lighting.

## Which fixes does the research support?
Cut videos into short segments. Philip Guo, Juho Kim and Rob Rubin analyzed 6.9 million video sessions across four edX courses in 2014. Median engagement was at most 6 minutes regardless of how long the video was, and students often made it less than halfway through videos longer than 9 minutes. The share of sessions followed by an attempt at the next problem fell from 56% for the shortest videos to 31% for the longest. Their recommendation: plan lessons in chunks under 6 minutes.
Put a question after every segment. In a 2013 PNAS study by Szpunar, Khan and Schacter, Harvard students watched a 21-minute statistics lecture split into four segments. Those quizzed after each segment reported mind-wandering on 19% of probes, against 39% for students shown the same questions with the answers filled in and 41% for students who did arithmetic instead. On the final test they scored 90%, against 76% and 68%. It was a lab study, but the mechanism is simple: a learner who knows a question is coming pays attention. Our guide to checking for understanding has twelve question formats to use.
Ask for a plan on day one. In three HarvardX courses, Michael Yeomans and Justin Reich added open-ended planning prompts at the start of the course. Completion rose 29% and certificate purchases 40%, most for students also enrolled in traditional schools. One odd result is worth knowing: learners whose plans focused on specific times were less likely to finish. Ask about obstacles and strategies, not just a calendar slot.
The honest caveat on nudges
When Kizilcec, Reich, Yeomans and colleagues tested established interventions across 247 courses from Harvard, MIT and Stanford, with about a quarter of a million students over 2.5 years, the self-regulation prompts raised engagement in the first few weeks but not final completion. The authors conclude that scaling interventions like these across many contexts can cut their average effect by an order of magnitude. Nudges are cheap and worth adding. They are not a strategy on their own.

## Do deadlines, cohorts and reminders help?
These are the fixes creators reach for first, and the evidence for them in self-paced courses is thinner than the research above. Treat them as good practice to test on your own cohorts, not as proven effects.

- Cohort start dates. A fixed start date turns “someday” into a date, and a group moving together gives learners someone to notice their absence. The cost is flexibility: people who enroll mid-cycle wait.
- Soft deadlines per module. A suggested finish date per module with a weekly “you’re on track” or “you’re one module behind” message. Keep it forgiving: a missed hard deadline hands the learner a reason to stop.
- Reminders that resume, not nag. “You stopped 3 minutes into lesson 5: ser for descriptions. Pick up where you left off” beats “We miss you.” Send it from what the learner did last, not on a fixed schedule.
- A small number that belongs to the learner. Lessons done this week, or a streak of study days. Keep it tied to learning, not to logins.

## Where does live help fit?
The stall point in the funnel above is rarely a motivation problem. It is a learner who watched the ser vs estar video twice, still can’t tell which to use, and has nobody to ask at the moment they are stuck. There are four ways to fix that, and each has a trade-off:

- Live office hours with the creator. The best help there is, and the one that does not scale: your evenings go first.
- A community forum or chat group. Cheap, and good for motivation, but answers arrive hours or days later, if at all.
- Teaching assistants. Fast and personal, at a cost per hour that grows with enrollment.
- An AI tutor on the hard chapters. Available at 11 pm and priced per use. It helps only if it teaches from your course, asks the learner questions and checks the answers; a chatbot that only answers questions can end up doing the learner’s thinking for them.
Size the job before you pick. In the illustrative funnel, 240 learners reach module 4. If each needs about 15 minutes of one-to-one help to get past it, that is 3,600 minutes, or 60 hours of a person’s time for one module in one cohort. The same minutes from an AI tutor priced per learner-minute cost $108 at $0.03 a minute (Tutezy’s rate). Neither number is large; the difference is that the person has to be available at the moment each learner gets stuck.
Whatever you choose, put it where your stall points are, not everywhere. We compare the recorded-course and live-tutor models in Tutezy vs recorded courses , and the three ways to add an AI tutor to an existing course in how to add an AI tutor to your online course .

## A 30-day plan to improve online course completion
Thirty days is too short to see final completion change, but long enough to move activation, unit-one completion and week-two retention for a new cohort. The plan:

- 1 Days 1–3: instrument the funnel
Log enrolled, started lesson, finished lesson and last active for every learner. Rebuild the funnel table above for your last cohort.

- 2 Days 4–7: find the stall points
Rank lessons by the share of learners who reach them but don’t finish. Read every question and comment posted on the top three.

- 3 Days 8–11: fix onboarding
Make lesson 1 short with an early win. Add an open-ended planning prompt to the welcome: how will you fit this in, and what might get in the way?

- 4 Days 12–17: split and quiz
Cut long videos at the stall points into segments under about 6 minutes, each followed by two or three questions.

- 5 Days 18–22: put help at the stall points
Office hours, a same-day answer target, or an AI tutor on those chapters. Measure time to an answer.

- 6 Days 23–26: add gentle accountability
Soft module deadlines, a weekly progress note, and resume reminders that name the exact lesson.

- 7 Days 27–30: compare cohorts
Set the new cohort’s activation, unit-one completion and week-two retention against the last cohort’s. Keep what moved; drop what didn’t.

If you sell to organizations rather than individuals, the same plan applies; the reminders come from a manager instead of an app. For turning existing material into shorter, question-led lessons, see turning PDFs, slides and videos into interactive lessons .
Where Tutezy fits

## What we built for this
Tutezy is aimed at the “stuck on one concept” exit. It compiles a creator’s recorded videos (transcribed), PDFs and slides into lessons, and adds a “learn with the teacher” button beside each chapter. The AI teacher explains on a whiteboard, asks a question after each concept, answers doubts from the course material, revisits weak concepts, and resumes with a recap if the learner leaves mid-lesson. It can speak in the creator’s cloned voice ($20 one-time). The creator sees completion and mastery per student per chapter, and weak concepts across the cohort, which shows which chapters need re-recording. It costs $0.03 per learner-minute, only while a learner is in a lesson. Details on Tutezy for course creators and pricing .
Where it is not the answer: it is not a plugin for Teachable, Kajabi or Thinkific. Courses run in the white-label Vacademy learner app on web, Android and iOS, with migration included, so switching platforms is part of the decision. It won’t fix a course learners don’t need, and courses that are mainly inspiration, with nothing to check, are a poor fit.

## Frequently asked questions
What is a good completion rate for an online course?+
There is no universal benchmark, because it depends on price, length and why people enrolled. For free MOOCs, Katy Jordan’s study of 221 courses found completion from 0.7% to 52.1%, with a median of 12.6%. At Harvard and MIT on edX, 46% of learners who paid for a verified certificate completed in 2017–18. Compare your course with its own previous cohorts rather than with a published average.

What is the average completion rate for MOOCs?+
Low. Reich and Ruipérez-Valiente’s 2019 analysis of Harvard and MIT courses on edX found that 3.13% of all participants completed in 2017–18. Jordan’s 2015 study of 221 MOOCs put the median at 12.6% of enrolled students. Completion is much higher among learners who pay: 46% of verified-certificate learners in the same Harvard and MIT data completed.

Why do students not finish online courses?+
The common reasons are lack of time, no one holding them accountable, long passive videos, and getting stuck on one concept with nobody to ask. Many learners also intend to finish but never turn the intention into a plan. The first two weeks matter most: in Jordan’s data, the share of active students levels out after weeks one and two.

How long should online course videos be?+
Short. In Guo, Kim and Rubin’s study of 6.9 million video sessions on edX, median engagement was at most 6 minutes regardless of video length, and students often watched less than half of videos longer than 9 minutes. They recommend segmenting videos into chunks under 6 minutes. Adding a few questions between segments also helps learners stay focused.

Do reminders and planning prompts improve course completion?+
Sometimes, modestly. Asking learners to write a plan at the start raised completion by 29% in three HarvardX courses. But when similar self-regulation prompts were tested across 247 courses with a quarter of a million students, they raised engagement in the first few weeks and not final completion. Use them, but don’t expect them to fix a course on their own.

What metrics should course creators track besides completion?+
Track activation (the share of enrollees who start lesson one within a week), unit-one completion, week-two retention, and the lesson where each learner last stopped. These move within days, show where learners stall, and tell you what to fix long before the final completion rate changes.

# How to choose AI tutoring software: 12 questions to ask
The right AI tutoring software teaches your own material accurately, checks each student’s understanding instead of only answering questions, and reports what every student learned, at a cost you can predict from your real usage. To choose one, ask every vendor the same 12 questions, score the answers against the red flags below, and run a two-week pilot with real students before you sign.
By the Tutezy team · September 25, 2026 · 12 min read

Key takeaways

- ✦ Accuracy starts with the source. Ask what the tutor teaches from, whether you can review a lesson before students see it, and what it does off-syllabus.
- ✦ Answering is not teaching. Look for a lesson plan, a check after each concept, hints before answers, and memory of each student.
- ✦ The report is the product for you. If you cannot see who understood what, you cannot act on it before the next class.
- ✦ Ask the data questions before the demo. Ownership, model training, deletion, and for US schools, FERPA and COPPA questions about minors.
- ✦ Price your real usage, not the list price. Model one term’s minutes or seats, then add setup, extras, minimums and platform fees.
In this article

- What AI tutoring software should do
- Content and accuracy (questions 1–3)
- Teaching (questions 4–6)
- Student experience (questions 7–8)
- Control and reporting (questions 9–10)
- Data and safety (question 11)
- Pricing and total cost (question 12)
- The scorecard
- A two-week pilot plan

## What should AI tutoring software actually do?
AI tutoring software uses a language model, usually with speech in and out, to teach a student one to one. For an organization (a school, a test-prep company, a course business, an L&D team) it has three jobs: teach your material without making things up, actually teach rather than wait for questions, and tell you what each student understood.
Most demos show a good conversation. Few show the other two jobs, and that is where products differ. The 12 questions below are grouped into six areas. Send them to every vendor in writing before the demo, then ask each one to show the answer live on a chapter you pick. Score each answer 0 (red flag), 1 (partial) or 2 (clear yes, shown live). A red flag on accuracy or data should rule a vendor out whatever the total.

## Content and accuracy: is it grounded in your material?
1. What exactly does the tutor teach from? There are three possible answers: the vendor’s own curriculum, the model’s general knowledge (sometimes plus the web), or the material you upload. If you teach your own syllabus, with your notation, your worked-example style and your exam format, only the third is a fit. Ask which formats it ingests (scanned PDFs, recorded video, slide decks, question banks) and what happens to equations and diagrams. Then hand over your messiest chapter, not the vendor’s sample.
2. Can a teacher review a lesson before a student sees it? If every session is generated fresh, there is nothing to review in advance; you can only audit transcripts after students have seen the mistakes. Ask whether there is a preview, whether a teacher can correct it, and whether the correction then holds for every student. Ask too what happens to reviewed lessons when the vendor switches to a newer model.
3. What happens when a student goes off-syllabus, or asks for something that is not in the material? A grounded tutor says the material does not cover it, answers from what is there, and returns to the lesson. Ask whether it browses the web and whether you can turn that off. Our post on keeping an AI tutor grounded has a 10-minute probe test you can run during the demo.

## Teaching: does it teach, or only answer?
4. Does it teach a planned lesson, or only respond to questions? A chatbot serves the students who already know what to ask. A tutor opens the chapter, explains a concept, asks a question and moves on only when the student is ready. Ask the vendor to start a lesson and stay silent for the first two minutes. See what the software does on its own.
5. How does it check understanding, and what happens after a wrong answer? Look for a question after each concept, graded against an expected answer or rubric, a hint before the answer, a limit on how many times it loops, and a later revisit of concepts the student missed. This matters more than it sounds. In a field experiment with nearly 1,000 high-school math students in Turkey, Hamsa Bastani and colleagues at the University of Pennsylvania found that a GPT-4 chat interface raised scores on practice problems by 48%, yet students who had used it scored 17% lower than a control group once access was removed. A version prompted to give hints instead of answers largely removed that harm (the study was published in PNAS in 2025). Our list of techniques for checking understanding online shows what good checks look like.
6. Does it remember each student? Across sessions, the tutor should keep where the student stopped, which concepts they have mastered and which mistakes they made, then resume with a short recap. “Each chat starts fresh” means every session repeats the diagnosis and nothing builds up for the student or for you.

## Student experience: voice, board, languages and devices
7. How does the student actually interact with it? A text chat is the minimum. Stronger products teach aloud, let the student answer by voice or by typing, and build a board step by step so a worked example unfolds instead of arriving as a wall of text. Check that formulas render properly, that diagrams are drawn rather than described, and that the student can slow the pace. Test on a mid-range phone with a real student, because long pauses make a spoken lesson hard to follow.
8. Which languages, devices and accessibility needs does it support? Ask for a live demo in every language you need rather than a list of supported languages. Ask where students use it: inside your existing platform, in the vendor’s app, or through a separate login. For accessibility, ask for a conformance report against the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines and test with a keyboard and a screen reader. US public schools and colleges have a deadline: the Department of Justice’s ADA Title II rule requires state and local government web content and mobile apps to meet WCAG 2.1 Level AA, and an April 2026 interim final rule moved compliance to April 26, 2027 for entities serving 50,000 people or more and April 26, 2028 for smaller ones. Check with your counsel on how it applies to you.

## Control and reporting: what can you set, and what comes back?
9. What can the organization control? Useful settings include tone or strictness, pace, the teacher persona and voice, which courses are switched on, session length, and whether the tutor may hand over full solutions. You should also be able to read the full transcript of any session. If something goes wrong with a student, “we can’t see the conversation” is not an answer you can give a parent or a client.
10. What does it report, and can you export it? The useful report is learning data: mastery per student per concept, the weak concepts across a class or batch, minutes taught and a session summary a teacher can read in a minute. Engagement dashboards (logins, messages sent) do not tell you who needs help. Ask for a CSV or API export so the data outlives the contract.

## Data and safety: who owns it, who trains on it, and what about minors?
11. Who owns your content and your students’ data, is any of it used to train models, and how are minors protected? Get written answers to each part. Who owns uploaded content and the lessons generated from it? Are content or transcripts used to train or fine-tune any model, the vendor’s or a third-party provider’s? Which AI providers receive data, and under what terms? How long is data kept, and how do you delete a learner or the whole account? Who inside the vendor can read transcripts? Which security certifications does the vendor hold (SOC 2, ISO 27001), and if none, what practices will it document for you? If the product clones a teacher’s voice or face, how is consent recorded and how is it revoked?
Questions to ask about minors’ data (US)
This is not legal advice. Use these to start the conversation with the vendor and your own counsel.
FERPA. Will the vendor sign an agreement under the school official exception? The Department of Education’s Privacy Technical Assistance Center lists the conditions: the vendor performs a function the school would otherwise use employees for, is under the school’s direct control for the use and maintenance of education records, and uses them only for authorized purposes without re-disclosing them. Ask whether the terms of service can change without notice; PTAC notes that unilateral changes make direct control hard to demonstrate.
COPPA. Is the product used by children under 13? FTC guidance says a school can consent on behalf of parents only when the data is used for a school-authorized educational purpose and no other commercial purpose. The FTC’s 2025 amendments to the COPPA Rule, with a compliance date of April 22, 2026, added separate parental consent for disclosures to third parties, a written data retention policy and a written information security program. Ask to see the vendor’s retention policy.

## Pricing and total cost: what will a real term cost?
12. What will one real term cost, all in? AI tutors are sold per seat (per enrolled student per month or year), per learner-minute of use, or as a platform fee plus usage. Give each vendor the same scenario, for example 200 students using it 30 minutes a week for 12 weeks, and ask for the full bill. Then ask about minimum commitments, annual prepayment, setup or content fees, extras (avatars, custom voices, extra languages), overages, platform fees if the tutor only runs inside the vendor’s app, and what it costs to export your data when you leave. Seat pricing charges for students who never log in; usage pricing charges only for use but needs a cap. Our AI tutor cost guide works through the arithmetic and a break-even calculation.

## The AI tutoring software scorecard
Copy this into a spreadsheet, one column per vendor. Score 0, 1 or 2 per row, and treat any red flag in rows 1–3 or 11 as a stop.
# | Question | Why it matters | Red-flag answer |

1 | What does it teach from? | Your syllabus, notation and method must survive | “It already knows everything” or “it searches the web” |
2 | Can we review a lesson first? | Errors are cheapest to fix before a student sees them | “Every session is generated fresh, so there’s nothing to review” |
3 | What happens off-syllabus? | An answer not drawn from your material is one nobody checked | “It will answer anything a student asks” |
4 | Does it teach a planned lesson? | A tutor that waits helps only the students who ask | “Students just ask it what they need” |
5 | How does it check and remediate? | Answer-giving can raise practice scores and lower test scores | “It explains the correct answer right away” |
6 | Does it remember each student? | Revisits and recaps need memory | “Each conversation starts fresh” |
7 | How does the student interact? | Voice, a board and diagrams teach; text walls don’t | A chat window only, with long pauses on a phone |
8 | Languages, devices, accessibility? | Every student has to be able to use it | A long language list but no live demo, and no accessibility report |
9 | What can we control and read? | You are accountable for what was said | “Transcripts aren’t available to customers” |
10 | What does it report and export? | Reports drive the next human lesson | Logins and message counts only; no export |
11 | Who owns and trains on the data? | Your content and minors’ data carry legal duties | “We may use data to improve our services,” with no opt-out or deletion path |
12 | What does a real term cost? | List prices hide minimums and extras | An annual commitment for every enrolled student before any pilot |

## How to run a two-week AI tutor pilot
A demo shows the vendor’s best case. A pilot shows yours. Two weeks is enough to test accuracy, participation, report quality and real cost. It is not enough to prove learning gains: the National Student Support Accelerator at Stanford describes high-impact tutoring as sessions three or more times a week for ten or more weeks. Treat the pilot as a gate to a longer, measured rollout.

- 1 Days 1–2: pick one chapter and one cohort
Choose a chapter students find hard, 20–50 students, and one teacher who will review the lessons and read the reports.

- 2 Days 2–3: review before launch
The teacher reviews every generated lesson and logs each error found. That count is your accuracy baseline.

- 3 Day 3: run the probe test
Ask off-syllabus questions, give a confident wrong answer, push back on a correct one, and ask for the answer outright. Record what happens.

- 4 Days 4–12: schedule the sessions
Three sessions a week of 20–30 minutes, on the timetable, not “optional”. Give students a pre-quiz of 10 questions on the chapter.

- 5 Day 8: read the reports
Does the weak-concept list match what the teacher sees in class? Read five transcripts in full, including one from a struggling student.

- 6 Days 13–14: decide on evidence
Run the post-quiz, total the cost, survey students and the teacher, and compare everything with the targets you set on day 1.

Success metrics to set before day 1
Accuracy: no uncorrected factual errors in reviewed lessons, and none found in the transcripts you read.
Participation: the share of invited students who complete at least four sessions (set your own target).
Understanding: pre-quiz to post-quiz change, ideally against a comparable group without the tutor.
Teacher trust: did the reports change what the teacher did in the next class, and would they assign it again?
Cost: actual cost per student-hour against the quote.

The live model does not author boards or browse the web; it grades answers against a rubric, gives hints, answers doubts about the material and adapts pace. Remediation loops are capped, weak concepts are revisited, and each student’s mastery per concept, the weak spots per batch and CSV exports come back to you. ## Frequently asked questions
What is AI tutoring software?+
AI tutoring software uses a language model, and often speech recognition and a synthetic voice, to teach a student one to one: it explains, asks a question, checks the answer and responds to mistakes. Products differ mainly in what they teach from (their own curriculum, general model knowledge or your material), whether they follow a lesson plan, and what they report back to the organization.

How do I evaluate an AI tutor for my school or training company?+
Send every vendor the same written questions about content accuracy, teaching method, student experience, control and reporting, data handling and total cost. Score the answers, then watch each shortlisted vendor convert one of your own hardest chapters in a live demo. Finish with a two-week pilot with real students and success metrics you set before it starts.

Is AI tutoring software FERPA compliant?+
FERPA compliance is not a certificate a product holds; it depends on how a school or district shares education records with the vendor and on the contract. Under the school official exception, the vendor must perform a function the school would otherwise use employees for, be under the school’s direct control for the use and maintenance of the records, and use them only for authorized purposes. This is not legal advice; involve your counsel or privacy officer.

Does COPPA apply to AI tutors used by children?+
COPPA applies to online services directed to children under 13, or that knowingly collect personal information from them. FTC guidance says a school can consent on behalf of parents only when the data is used for a school-authorized educational purpose and no other commercial purpose. The FTC’s 2025 amendments to the COPPA Rule had a compliance date of April 22, 2026, so ask vendors how they changed their practices.

How long should an AI tutoring pilot run?+
Two weeks is enough to test accuracy, participation, the quality of reports and real cost, but it is too short to prove learning gains. The National Student Support Accelerator describes high-impact tutoring as sessions three or more times a week for ten or more weeks, so plan a longer measured rollout after a pilot passes.

What is the difference between an AI tutor and an AI chatbot?+
A chatbot waits for a question and answers it. A tutor follows a plan: it explains a concept, asks the student a question, grades the answer, gives a hint when the student is wrong and comes back to weak concepts later. For an organization, the tutor should also report what each student understood.

# How much does an AI tutor cost? Pricing models compared | Tutezy

Buyer's guide

# How much does an AI tutor cost? Pricing models compared
AI tutor cost ranges from a few dollars per student per month on a consumer seat plan to a few cents per learner-minute on usage pricing. For a 100-student cohort learning 30 minutes a week for 12 weeks (36,000 minutes), that is $1,080 at $0.03 a minute, against $21,000 to $36,000 for the same 600 hours of one-to-one human tutoring at $35 to $60 an hour.
By the Tutezy team · September 25, 2026 · 11 min read

Key takeaways

- ✦ Four pricing models. Per seat, per learner-minute, build your own on AI APIs, and human tutoring by the hour. Each wins in a different situation.
- ✦ Per seat charges for enrollment; per minute charges for use. Divide the seat price by the per-minute rate to get the break-even minutes per student.
- ✦ Building your own is mostly an engineering bill. The voice API may cost a few cents a minute; the developers cost far more.
- ✦ Private human tutoring costs roughly 19 to 33 times more per hour but buys judgment and relationship. Price the hours you actually need a human for.
- ✦ Budget the hidden costs. Review time, minimums, extras, platform fees and data export rarely appear on the price page.
In this article

- How much an AI tutor costs
- The four pricing models
- Per-seat licenses
- Per-minute usage pricing
- Building your own
- AI tutor vs human tutor cost
- Worked example: 100 students, 12 weeks
- Per seat vs per minute: break-even
- Hidden costs to budget

## How much does an AI tutor cost?
AI tutor cost depends less on the product than on how it is priced. The same student using a tutor 30 minutes a week can cost you $3.90 a month on per-minute pricing at $0.03, a flat fee on a seat license whether they log in or not, or several hundred dollars a term with a human tutor. The only reliable way to compare is to take one realistic usage scenario and price it under every model.
This guide does that for a 100-student cohort, with the arithmetic shown so you can swap in your own numbers. All prices are as of September 2026 and come from each vendor’s or organization’s own page, listed at the end.

-
-
-
- $0$10k$20k$30kAI tutor$0.03/min: $1,080AI tutor + avatar$0.05/min: $1,800Seat license (example)$10/month: $3,000Small-group tutorswages only: $4,200–$12,000Private 1:1 tutor$35–$60/hr: $21,000–$36,000
Cost of 36,000 learner-minutes (100 students × 30 minutes a week × 12 weeks). Light segments show the top of a range. Human figures use Wyzant’s published average price range and the NSSA’s per-pupil-hour tutor wage estimates (wages only). The seat price is an illustrative example, not a quote.

## What are the four AI tutoring pricing models?
Almost every option you will be quoted fits one of four models. The reference points below are published prices, not negotiated quotes, and they are for different products, so use them to understand the shape of each model rather than to pick a vendor.
Model | How you pay | Published reference point (Sept 2026) | Suits | Watch for |

Per seat or license | A fixed fee per enrolled student per month or year | Khanmigo: $4/month or $44/year for learners and parents; free for teachers; districts on request | Heavy, steady use by most students | Paying for students who never log in; annual minimums |
Per learner-minute | Only the minutes a student is actually taught | Tutezy: $0.03/minute, $0.05 with an avatar shown | Uneven or seasonal use; pilots | No natural ceiling; set a cap per student or course |
Build your own | AI API usage plus engineering and hosting | OpenAI gpt-realtime-2.1 audio: $32 input, $64 output per 1M tokens | Teams with engineers and an unusual need | Salaries, maintenance, safety testing, model changes |
Human tutoring | Per hour of a tutor’s time | Wyzant: $35–$60/hour average; NSSA: $1,200–$2,500 per student per year for district programs | Mentoring, motivation, open-ended work | Scarce hours; one student or a small group at a time |

## Per-seat and per-student licenses
A seat license charges a fixed amount per enrolled student, usually per month or per year, whatever each student does. It is easy to budget and easy to approve. A well-known published consumer price is Khanmigo, Khan Academy’s AI tutor: as of September 2026 its pricing page lists $4 a month or $44 a year for learners and parents, free access for teachers, and quoted pricing for districts. Khanmigo teaches on Khan Academy’s own content, so treat that as a price reference, not a like-for-like quote for tutoring on your material.
The catch with seats is that you pay for enrollment, not learning. Every student on the roster costs the same whether they use the tutor daily or never open it. Before signing, ask what usage the vendor sees across similar customers, whether unused seats can be reassigned, and whether the contract has a minimum seat count or an annual term.

## Per-minute usage pricing
Usage pricing charges for each learner-minute of live tutoring. Tutezy, for example, charges $0.03 per learner-minute, or $0.05 while an animated teacher avatar is on screen, from prepaid credits, with no seat licenses or minimums. A student who never logs in costs nothing, which makes pilots and seasonal courses (exam prep, onboarding cohorts) cheap to run. The how it works page explains why a lesson compiled in advance keeps the live cost per minute low.
The trade-off is that the bill grows with use and has no natural ceiling. Ask three questions of any per-minute vendor: what exactly counts as a minute (idle time, reading notes afterwards), which features change the rate, and whether you can cap minutes per student or per course. A fixed session length per course, say 20 minutes, is the simplest cap.
To forecast a per-minute bill, multiply three numbers you can estimate: students who will actually use it, sessions per student per week, and minutes per session. A pilot gives you the first number, which is the hardest one to guess.

## What does it cost to build your own AI tutor?
Building your own means paying an AI provider per use and paying engineers to turn the model into a tutor. The API part is easy to estimate. OpenAI’s pricing page, as of September 2026, lists gpt-realtime-2.1 at $32 per million audio input tokens and $64 per million audio output tokens, and $10 and $20 for the mini model. OpenAI’s cost guide says user audio is 1 token per 100 ms and assistant audio 1 token per 50 ms, so a minute of student speech is 600 tokens and a minute of tutor speech is 1,200.
Take a minute in which the tutor speaks for 36 seconds and the student for 24 (a simplifying assumption with no silence):

- Tutor audio: 720 tokens × $64 per million = $0.046
- Student audio: 240 tokens × $32 per million = $0.008
- Total: about $0.054 per minute, or about $0.017 on the mini model
That is before the costs that grow during a conversation. OpenAI’s guide notes that the entire conversation is sent to the model for each response, so later turns cost more (cached input is much cheaper, which helps). Your instructions and course material add text tokens on every turn, and you still need speech hosting, storage and monitoring.
Then there is engineering. The US Bureau of Labor Statistics puts the median software developer wage at $135,980 a year (May 2025), about $11,330 a month before benefits and overhead. Three months of one developer is roughly $34,000 in salary alone, which is more than 30 terms of the per-minute cohort below.
And a voice connection is not yet a tutor. You would still need to turn your material into lessons, keep the model from inventing content, grade answers consistently, decide when to give a hint and when to move on, store each student’s progress, build teacher reports, and re-test all of it every time the provider ships a new model. Building makes sense when the tutor itself is your product, not when you need one for a course.

## AI tutor vs human tutor: what does each cost?
For private one-to-one tutoring, the US marketplace Wyzant says the average price of a tutor on its platform is between $35 and $60 an hour (in a December 2024 post), with higher rates in some subjects. At $0.03 a minute, an AI tutor costs $1.80 per student-hour, so the human hour costs roughly 19 to 33 times more.
For schools and districts, the National Student Support Accelerator (NSSA) at Stanford publishes program-level estimates. It says cost estimates for high-impact tutoring programs range from $1,000 to over $3,000 per pupil, and that districts should expect roughly $1,200 to $2,500 per student. Its budget guide lists tutor wages of $15–$20 an hour for novice tutors, $20–$30 for experienced tutors and $40–$60 for master tutors, which the guide converts to about $7–$20 per pupil-hour depending on group size and tutor type.
Price per hour is not the whole comparison. A human tutor brings judgment, motivation and a relationship (our post on Bloom’s 2 sigma problem covers what the research on tutoring says). The practical question is which hours need a human. Our Tutezy vs human tutoring comparison lays out where each one wins.

## Worked example: a 100-student cohort for 12 weeks
One hundred students each use a tutor for 30 minutes a week for a 12-week term. That is 100 × 30 × 12 = 36,000 learner-minutes, or 600 student-hours.
Option | Arithmetic | Total for the term | Per student |

AI tutor, per minute | 36,000 × $0.03 | $1,080 (plus a $20 voice clone: $1,100) | $10.80 |
AI tutor with avatar, per minute | 36,000 × $0.05 | $1,800 (plus a $20 voice clone: $1,820) | $18.00 |
AI tutor, per seat (example $10/month) | 100 × $10 × 3 months | $3,000, whatever the usage | $30.00 |
Build your own, audio tokens only | 36,000 × $0.017 to $0.054 | About $605–$1,935, plus engineering | $6–$19, plus engineering |
Small-group human tutors, wages only | 600 × $7 to $20 per pupil-hour | $4,200–$12,000 | $42–$120 |
Private one-to-one tutor | 600 × $35 to $60 | $21,000–$36,000 | $210–$360 |

Two caveats keep this honest. The per-minute AI figures also carry a small one-time cost to prepare lessons (Tutezy’s pricing page puts a typical 40-slide course at under $2.50). And the human rows buy something the AI rows do not, so the fair reading is not “AI is 20 times cheaper” but “every student can get the practice loop, and the human hours can go where they matter most.”

## Per seat vs per minute: where is the break-even?
The break-even formula
Break-even minutes per student per month = seat price per month ÷ price per minute. Below that usage, per-minute pricing is cheaper; above it, the seat is cheaper. Divide by 4.33 to get minutes per week.

Seat price per student per month | Break-even at $0.03/min | Break-even at $0.05/min |

$4 (a low consumer price point) | 133 min/month (about 31 a week) | 80 min/month (about 18 a week) |
$10 | 333 min/month (about 77 a week) | 200 min/month (about 46 a week) |
$20 | 667 min/month (about 154 a week) | 400 min/month (about 92 a week) |

The average can mislead when usage is uneven. Suppose 30 of your 100 students use the tutor 300 minutes a month and the other 70 use it 30 minutes. At $0.03 a minute that is (30 × 300 + 70 × 30) × $0.03 = $333 a month. A $10 seat for all 100 is $1,000. Per-seat pricing wins only when average use per student is above the break-even, so pull a month of real usage from a pilot before you decide. Our AI tutoring software buyer’s checklist covers the pilot.

## Hidden costs to budget

- Content preparation and review. Someone has to supply the material and check what the tutor will teach. Multiply the teacher hours per chapter by your own staff cost.
- Onboarding and platform fees. If the tutor only runs inside the vendor’s app or platform, that platform may have its own price, and students need accounts.
- Minimum commitments. Annual terms, minimum seat counts, prepaid tiers and auto-renewal clauses.
- Overages and caps. What happens above a fair-use limit on a seat plan, or when a per-minute cohort uses more than planned.
- Extras. Avatars, custom voices, extra languages and premium support, sometimes priced separately.
- Regeneration. Some products charge again when you rebuild a lesson after changing the source.
- Taxes. Published prices may exclude sales tax; Khanmigo’s page says its prices do.
- Data export and exit. Whether transcripts and reports export as CSV at no charge, and what happens to them when you leave.
The quote request to send every vendor
“We have [100] students. We expect each to use the tutor about [30] minutes a week for a [12]-week term, with [half] using a voice or avatar feature. Please send the total cost for that term, itemized, including: setup or onboarding, content preparation, any platform or account fees, one-time charges for voices or avatars, minimum commitments and contract length, what happens above our expected usage, taxes, and the cost of exporting our transcripts and reports if we leave.”
Put every reply into the worked-example table above. Quotes that will not itemize are hard to compare, and that is worth knowing too.

If you are running a tutoring business rather than buying for a school, the same arithmetic drives your margins; see how to scale a tutoring business with AI .
Where Tutezy fits

## What we built for this
Tutezy uses the per-minute model: $0.03 per learner-minute, $0.05 while the animated avatar is shown, $20 one-time per cloned teacher voice, $100 one-time for a custom avatar (stock avatars are free), and a small one-time compile cost per slide that is shown before you convert anything. Credits are prepaid, there are no seat licenses or minimums, volume pricing starts above 1,000 students, and every credit is itemized per course and per student. In India the rates are ₹3 and ₹5 a minute, plus GST. The full rate card and worked examples are on the pricing page .
It is not always the cheapest option. If most of your students would use a tutor for hours every day, run the break-even above; a flat seat license may cost less. Tutezy runs inside the Vacademy learner app, so an organization not yet on Vacademy is onboarded first, and Vacademy’s own platform pricing is separate. It does not replace a human tutor for mentoring or motivation; see Tutezy vs human tutoring .

## Frequently asked questions
How much does an AI tutor cost per month?+
It depends on the pricing model. Consumer plans cost a few dollars a month; Khanmigo, for example, lists $4 a month or $44 a year for learners and parents as of September 2026. School and district licenses are usually quoted on request, and per-minute tutors bill only for use: at $0.03 a minute, a student who learns 30 minutes a week costs about $3.90 a month.

Is an AI tutor cheaper than a human tutor?+
Per hour, by a wide margin. At $0.03 a minute an AI tutor costs $1.80 per student-hour, while Wyzant puts the average price of a tutor on its marketplace at $35 to $60 an hour. A human tutor still does things an AI tutor cannot, such as mentoring, motivation and open-ended project work, so many organizations use both.

How much does it cost to build your own AI tutor?+
At OpenAI’s September 2026 list prices for gpt-realtime-2.1, the audio alone for a spoken tutoring minute works out to roughly five cents under simple assumptions, or under two cents on the mini model, before the conversation history is re-sent each turn and before hosting. The larger cost is engineering: the US Bureau of Labor Statistics puts the median software developer wage at $135,980 a year (May 2025).

What is per-minute AI tutor pricing?+
You pay for each minute a student spends in a live tutoring session, instead of a fee for every enrolled student. It suits uneven or seasonal use and pilots, because students who never log in cost nothing. Check what counts as a minute, whether features like an avatar cost more per minute, and whether there are minimums.

What are the hidden costs of AI tutoring software?+
The common ones are staff time to prepare and review content, onboarding, minimum commitments and annual prepayment, overage charges, paid extras such as avatars and custom voices, platform fees when the tutor only runs inside the vendor’s app, charges to regenerate content, sales tax, and the cost of exporting your data when you leave.

How much does high-impact tutoring cost per student?+
The National Student Support Accelerator at Stanford says cost estimates for high-impact tutoring programs range from $1,000 to over $3,000 per pupil, and that districts should expect to spend roughly $1,200 to $2,500 per student. Those figures assume sessions at least three times a week, so they buy far more hours than a light AI tutoring schedule.
